title: The LaFountaine Brain Paradox (v1.5): Finite Biological Substrates and Unbounded Internal Representational Dynamics
abstract: Description This record presents Version 1.5 of The LaFountaine Brain Paradox, a foundational interdisciplinary framework examining how a finite biological system can support unbounded internal representational and computational dynamics without violating anatomical or physical constraints. The framework formally distinguishes between (i) the finite physical substrate of the brain, modeled as a bounded anatomical domain; (ii) an infinite-dimensional internal representational state space, capturing the structure of possible cognitive configurations; and (iii) recursive internal dynamics, modeled abstractly by an operator governing state evolution over time. Unboundedness is defined strictly in representational terms via norm-based state-space trajectories and does not imply infinite physical resources, storage, or energy. Version 1.5 constitutes a stabilized foundational release. It includes a formal mathematical statement, explicit scope limitations, methodological clarification, versioning discipline, and supporting technical and audit documentation. title: AI Topics Module 2: Education
abstract: This textbook module examines the intersection of cognitive neuroscience, pedagogy, and artificial intelligence as they converge in the secondary school classroom. Beginning with the theory of mental rigor — the disciplined, sustained exertion of focused cognitive effort as a biological process with measurable neural correlates — the text argues that understanding how the brain learns and understanding how AI systems learn are not separate intellectual projects but deeply connected ones. Each chapter weaves AI concepts explicitly into its treatment of the neuroscience of learning, establishing structural parallels between biological and artificial intelligence that deepen understanding of both. Chapter One presents culturally responsive classroom activities — including probabilistic choice games, biometric data analysis, memory exercises, and kinesthetic geometry — and connects each to foundational AI concepts including classification, feature engineering, sequence processing, and convolutional neural networks. title: Sleep Deprivation, Memory Consolidation, and Cognitive Function: A Neuroscience Analysis
abstract: Although the negative effects of sleep deprivation on learning, memory and executive function are well-known, an increasing number of studies have put forward that these impairments are mainly due to a disturbance in sleep-dependent memory consolidation rather than fatigue alone. This paper investigates the connection between sleep and memory and cognition, examines how the brain processes information during sleep to promote learning, and enhances high-order thinking skills. Currently, it has been shown that memories formed in a waking state are organised during sleep through cooperation among the hippocampus, neocortex and prefrontal cortex. Meanwhile, there is temporal coupling between the cortical slow oscillations, thalamocortical sleep spindles and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples which collectively promote hippocampal replay and cortical plasticity and drive a redistribution of newly acquired information through long-term cortical networks. Synaptic homeostasis which keeps the brain efficient and prevents the loss of learning capability also mentioned in this review. title: Editorial: Optical interrogation of the nervous system: recent advances in optical techniques and their applications
abstract: The nervous system consists of a huge number of neurons and non-neuronal cells. To understand brain function, fine-scale analysis of both brain-wide structure and functions of neural circuits is essential. To achieve this, optical methods are useful. Recently, fluorescent probes for calcium, membrane potential, neurotransmitters and intracellular signals have been developed (Aggarwal et al., 2023;Bando et al., 2019Bando et al., , 2021;;Yokoyama et al., 2024). The Application of microbial opsins in neuroscience has enabled spatiotemporally precise manipulation of neuronal activity (Fenno et al., 2011). Furthermore, technical advances in microscopy have also contributed to neuroscience. The use of femtosecond pulse laser enabled multiphoton excitation which achieved high signal-to-noise ratio and deep penetration in scattering tissues (Denk et al., 1990). Combination of multiphoton microscopy and spatial light modulator allowed optical stimulation of neurons with desired patterns together with imaging neural activity (Yang et al., 2018). title: Editorial: High-altitude neuroscience: innovative pathways from adaptive mechanisms to health management
abstract: High-altitude (HA) environments, conventionally defined as elevations above 2,500 m, provide a distinctive natural setting for investigating how the human brain responds to sustained environmental stress. Reduced barometric pressure and oxygen availability coexist with cold, aridity, ultraviolet radiation, and large diurnal temperature variation, placing substantial demands on physiological homeostasis (Chroboczek et al., 2021;Virues-Ortega et al., 2004). The brain is particularly sensitive because of its high and continuous energy requirements (Raichle, 2010;Raichle & Gusnard, 2002;Yan, 2014). Yet HA exposure cannot be understood as a simple progression from hypoxia to dysfunction. Depending on dose, duration, developmental stage, genetic background, health status, and prior acclimatization, neural responses may encompass stress, compensation, adaptation, resilience, vulnerability, and, under selected conditions, therapeutic plasticity. Several contributions clarify why apparently successful acclimatization may coexist with biological cost. Gong et al. title: Tactile Learning: The Neuroscience Behind Braille and Touch Perception
abstract: Introduction: For those who are blind and rely on touch instead of vision, braille is a vital reading and communication tool. Research indicates that the brain adjusts by reallocating visual processing areas to improve touch perception and reading efficiency as the fingertips grow more sensitive with continued use.  Methods: Studies reveal that this neural plasticity improves the somatosensory cortex’s ability to recognize tactile patterns. Numerous technologies, including digital Braille displays and vibration-based feedback tools, have been developed to aid in the learning of Braille.  Results: Both reading accuracy and accessibility are enhanced by these devices. The potential for improving tactile literacy is high for tools that replicate realistic skin-texture interactions. Camera-based readers, which may be hampered by alignment problems and inadequate lighting, are frequently outperformed by pressure-sensitive pads.  Discussion: Insights into brain plasticity can inform the design of more effective teaching and reading aids for the blind. title: The explanatory ground of the brainbound view of consciousness: A reply to enactive embodied externalism
Editorial: Neural mechanisms of sensory-motor integration in manual tasks
abstract: For much of the history of psychology and neuroscience, the brain was commonly conceived as an input-output system that receives information from the environment, constructs internal representations of the world, and generates appropriate motor commands. This classical picture has progressively evolved, echoing ideas first anticipated by von Helmholtz more than a century ago (1924). Contemporary cognitive neuroscience increasingly views the brain as a homeostatic organ, whose primary function is not to faithfully interpret the external world, but to maintain the organism's integrity through adaptive interactions with its environment (Friston, 2010). Within this framework, neural processing is fundamentally predictive: the brain relies on internal generative models to infer the hidden causes of sensory signals, predict the sensory consequences of action, anticipate future states of the body and the environment, and continuously update these models by minimizing prediction errors (Rao and Ballard, 1999).The predictive perspective has also reshaped theories of motor control (Franklin and Wolpert, 2011;Floegel et al., 2023;Priorelli et al., 2024). title: The Neuroscience of Religious and Spiritual Experiences: Focus on Methodological Issues
abstract: Abstract The aim of this chapter is to provide a perspective on the current state of research that assesses spiritual experiences and their neurobiological correlates specifically focusing on the methodological challenges of this field of research. Current research studies have utilized both first-person and third-person approaches towards understanding spiritual experiences. In addition, studies of pathological conditions and the effects of psychedelic compounds on spiritual experiences are also important to consider. All these studies have helped to elucidate the underlying neurobiological mechanisms related to spiritual experiences. Overall, this field of study attempting to link the brain and spiritual experiences, sometimes referred to as neurotheology, has a bright and exciting future.

title: Brainana: an end-to-end preprocessing framework for macaque neuroimaging
NeuralRNN: a unified framework for recurrent neural network methods in cognitive neuroscience
abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a central tool in neuroscience to optimize cognitive tasks and reconstruct dynamical systems. Around these two paradigms, many RNN model variants have been tailored to capture specific computations of the brain. In practice, however, this methodological diversity remains difficult to exploit, because different paradigms and model variants are mostly implemented in idiosyncratic, study-specific code. Here we introduce NeuralRNN, an open-source Python framework that unifies these paradigms and model variants in a general-purpose pipeline. NeuralRNN brings task optimization, dynamical system reconstruction, and biological constraints into a single objective interface. It also provides an integrated and extensible model library spanning generic, structure-constrained, gain-modulated, and gated RNNs. Furthermore, data, models, and training are constructed through a shared automated pipeline and are equipped with a suite of tools for dynamical systems analysis. Together, NeuralRNN lowers the barrier to implementing, comparing, and extending RNN methods in neuroscience.

title: W140. A SPATIAL TRANSCRIPTOMICS ANALYSIS PIPELINE FOR CELL-TYPE-SPECIFIC PROFILING OF COCAINE-INDUCED GENE EXPRESSION
abstract: Background Cocaine use disorder (CUD) drives persistent alterations in neural circuits and gene expression underlying compulsive drug-seeking and relapse. While cocaine induces widespread transcriptional changes across cortico-striatal reward circuitry, their spatial organization within intact tissue remains poorly understood. Prior single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies lack spatial resolution, limiting region- and cell-type-specific mapping. Single-cell spatial transcriptomics enables gene expression characterization within intact tissue architecture. Here, we developed and applied an analysis pipeline to identify cocaine-responsive cell populations and map their transcriptional changes across the circuitry. Methods Nine-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were subjected to saline (n = 2) or cocaine conditioning (n = 2; 10 mg/kg for 3 days). Cocaine-seeking behavior was confirmed using the conditioned place preference paradigm. Brains were then perfused, fixed in neutral buffered formalin, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned at 5 μm. title: Neurobiological Cognitive Integration (NCI): The Autonomic Brief, the Budget That Constrains It, and the Life It Renders
abstract: What we know. The human nervous system takes in roughly a billion bits of sensory information per second; conscious awareness receives about ten. The rest is processed below awareness — largely what we call the subconscious — where it regulates the body and directs behavior. What reaches awareness is a compressed summary, which we call the autonomic brief, and it arrives with little record of what was left out, or why. Who decides. Not the person, at least not consciously. The choosing is done before awareness, governed by settings that were in place long before anyone could have chosen them, and the brief carries no sign that a choice was made. Everyone lives inside a selection they did not make and cannot directly see, and no two people's selections are made the same way. The question. How are ten chosen from a billion? Why do two people given the same information come away with different summaries, each sure that theirs is simply the truth? Why can the same person, rested and exhausted, seem like two different people? title: BRIDGING GENETIC DISCOVERY AND THERAPY: TRANSLATIONAL STUDIES TO FINE-MAPPING PTSD RISK AND MECHANISMS
abstract: Overall Abstract Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a complex psychiatric condition shaped by genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. Despite rapid advances in genomic discovery, translating association signals into biological mechanisms and therapeutic strategies remains a central challenge. This symposium representing the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium PTSD (PGC-PTSD) working group will be chaired by Profs. Nikolaos Daskalakis (Boston University) and Caroline Nievergelt (UCSD), integrates statistical genetics, functional genomics, and translational neuroscience to advance our understanding of PTSD. The first presentation by Dr. Adam Maihofer (Assistant Professor @ UCSD) reports findings from the PGC-PTSD, including the largest GWAS of PTSD (> 3 million participants, > 500K cases) and the first well-powered rare variant association study (RVAS; > 700K participants). Over 300 genome-wide significant loci and 500 genes enriched for synaptic pathways were identified. Strikingly, the top RVAS genes—TET2, ASXL1, and DNMT3A—are epigenetic modifiers regulating DNA methylation, converging with GWAS findings to highlight gene–environment interactions in PTSD etiology. title: Editorial: Animal communication: neurobiological, chemical, and physiological aspects
abstract: Animal communication underlies many of the interactions through which animals acquire information, coordinate social behavior, avoid predators, compete for resources, and reproduce successfully. Since the foundations of modern ethology were established, communication has been interpreted within a broader biological framework in which behavior is understood through its causation, development, function, and evolutionary history (1). Building on this foundation, evolutionary theories of animal signaling established that communication is shaped by natural selection through the dynamic interaction between signal production and receiver responses, both of which contribute to the evolution and maintenance of signaling systems (2,3). This conceptual framework was further refined by recognizing that communication emerges from the interaction between signalers and receivers, whose behavioral responses actively determine the biological significance of signals (4). Complementing this perspective, communication has also been viewed as a process through which signals influence receiver behavior, extending classical information-based interpretations of animal signaling (5). title: Navigating the New World of Neuroscience: From Biological Plasticity to Theological Reflection
abstract: This article surveys the transformative shift in neuroscience from traditional models of fixed brain architecture to a contemporary understanding of neuroplasticity, lifelong neurogenesis, and computational advances. It reviews core developments including synaptic and structural plasticity, adult neurogenesis, cutting-edge imaging and stimulation technologies, and the genetic revolution driving new clinical interventions. The convergence of neurology and psychiatry is discussed alongside the concept of the individual connectome, highlighting the unique interplay of genetic and environmental factors in shaping brain function. Societal implications extend to neuro-humanities, neuroeducation, corporate applications, and consumer neuro-technologies, raising ethical questions around privacy, identity, and regulatory oversight. The article further explores the epistemological limits of neuroscience and integrates a Christian theological perspective, advocating for intellectual humility and a holistic anthropology that recognises the spiritual dimensions of scientific discovery. title: From Generation to Access: On Artificial Dreaming as an Advanced Form of AI Art
abstract: The convergence of generative artificial intelligence and brain-computer interface technology is pushing artificial dreaming from science fiction into the scope of academic inquiry. Existing research has focused primarily on technical implementation pathways and sensory fidelity goals; while fragmented ethical and risk warnings exist, there remains a lack of systematic assessment of the physiological costs that artificial dreaming imposes on core sleep functions, a scarcity of theoretical refinement grounded in the dream system's own generative rules and aesthetic nature, and an absence of clear demarcation between different application paradigms. Taking a complete REM sleep–awakening boundary consciousness experience as its phenomenological point of departure, this paper draws on sleep neuroscience and neuroaesthetics to develop a theoretical inference that distills four layers of constraint in the human dream system: the visual bias of PGO wave conduction pathways, the functional auditory suppression of thalamic gating's "external-open, internal-closed" strategy, the emotional safety threshold of the auditory–amygdala short pathway, and the gating leakage effect during sleep-boun

title: Relational Novelty-Driven Cognitive Encoding and Worldview Transformation Theory (RNCE-WTT)
abstract: This paper proposes a unified cross-disciplinary theoretical framework that models human cognition, perception, memory encoding, and worldview transformation as a novelty-driven, pattern-recognition-based system. The theory integrates concepts from neuroscience, cognitive science, psychology, philosophy, and information theory to formalize how experiential uniqueness (novelty/rarity) governs psychological encoding and perspective evolution. The proposed framework formalizes the brain as a probabilistic inference engine that evaluates incoming stimuli relative to stored experiential priors, thereby assigning cognitive salience proportional to informational novelty. This document develops a mathematical, philosophical, and neurocognitive synthesis that explains how worldviews emerge, stabilize, and transform through iterative experiential comparisons.

title: Editorial: Theoretical and computational insights into brain-based cognition
abstract: Understanding how cognitive functions emerge from the activity of the brain remains one of the central challenges of contemporary neuroscience. Cognition depends on processes occurring across multiple spatial and temporal scales, from the dynamics of individual neurons and local circuits to coordinated activity among distributed brain regions. Theoretical and computational approaches are therefore essential not only for describing neural activity, but also for identifying principles that can connect these different levels of organization and ultimately relate neural dynamics to perception, memory, behavior, and other cognitive functions.The Research Topic Theoretical and Computational Insights into Brain-Based Cognition was conceived to bring together complementary perspectives on this problem. The five contributions illustrate the diversity of approaches currently available, ranging from statistical analysis of large-scale electrophysiological recordings to mathematical descriptions of neuronal dynamics and broader conceptual frameworks concerning neural communication and emergence. title: Neurostimulation in the treatment of psychiatric disorders: Underlying mechanisms and critical analysis of circuit-based interventions
abstract: Neurostimulation of targeted brain regions has emerged as a novel therapeutic approach to induce remission in patients with various psychiatric disorders. This strategy encompasses several modalities, including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and transcranial focused ultrasound neurostimulation (tFUS), all of which aim to modulate dysfunctional neural circuits and restore activity toward physiological ranges. While the clinical efficacy of these techniques is increasingly documented, the mechanisms underlying their effects—beyond immediate changes in regional excitability—remain incompletely understood. Further, neurostimulation represents not only a technical advance, but also a conceptual shift in psychiatry, moving from interventions aimed at modulating neurotransmission or cognition toward circuit-based models of mental illness. This review surveys the current literature to clarify the mechanisms of action of neurostimulation across multiple levels of biological integration, ranging from large-scale neural circuits to cellular and subcellular processes. title: Zero-shot evaluations expose structured generalization limits in predictive models of the brain
abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) can predict neural responses to natural images with remarkable accuracy, making them promising models of human vision. However, prediction scores alone reveal little about what computations these models have captured or how well they generalize beyond the images on which they are trained. Here, we introduce a principled zero-shot model evaluation framework in which ANN-based encoding models are frozen before being tested on not just held out images but entirely new datasets. Our strongest tests repurpose decades of cognitive neuroscience experiments as diagnostic benchmarks for identifying which computations current models capture and where they fail. To implement this framework we built encoding models of human category-selective regions (FFA, PPA, and EBA) using several pretrained ANNs and evaluated these fixed models across 7 independent fMRI datasets and 31 cognitive experiments from 10 published studies. This framework revealed three broad patterns. First, zero-shot evaluations exposed systematic limits to model predictivity that were largely hidden by standard within-dataset cross-validation. title: Who Controls the Future? Federico Faggin, Odam Tili & the Academic War on Free Thought
abstract: What if mathematics can describe the brain—but never fully explain consciousness? In this provocative discovery documentary, we examine the striking intersection between Federico Faggin’s reflections on consciousness, mathematics and free will, and the conclusions associated with Odam Tili—a framework that places human meaning, self-awareness and intellectual freedom at the center of the discussion. Faggin argues that mathematics is a product of consciousness. If consciousness created mathematics, can mathematics alone explain the nature of consciousness? And if the future is shaped by free will, can any system truly predict and control it? This film investigates the deeper connection between: • Neuroscience and human meaning• Mathematics and consciousness• Prediction and power• Grant-funded academia and intellectual freedom• Institutional blindness and deliberate suppression• Odam Tili and the next revolution in human thinking The central question is not whether science is wrong. The question is whether science becomes incomplete when the human being is reduced to a measurable object. title: Universal Living-System Consent, Personhood, Identity, Restitution & Recoverability: Terminal Mechanism and Architecture Closure
abstract: This publication develops a universal living-system architecture for protecting personhood, consent, identity, evidence, responsibility, recoverability, and future possibility across materially consequential transitions. The framework treats the human person as a multidimensional living continuity system spanning physical and biological state, brain and nervous-system activity, cognition, consciousness-associated states, identity, agency, emotion, relationships, family continuity, information, digital representations, derived models, economic dependencies, technological interfaces, infrastructure, and successor states. Consent is modeled as a living, time-indexed and purpose-bounded state rather than a permanent binary authorization. Observation, inference, prediction, intervention, experimentation, commercialization, model training, transfer, automation, publication, physical actuation, and successor use remain distinguishable transitions. Permission for one does not silently authorize another. A major extension addresses identity under technological integration. title: SN12 — Neural Dynamics and Embodied Cognitive Architecture: Physical Interface, Stabilization, Distortion, and Restoration
abstract: SN12: Neural Dynamics and Embodied Cognitive Architecture develops the Structural Neuroscience account of the physical brain as an embodied interface participating in cognition while remaining ontologically distinct from Soul / Mind. Document class: Canon — Structural Neuroscience. The volume distinguishes essential cognitive Configuration from changing physical neural configuration, operative access from essential identity, dynamic stabilization from native frozen equilibrium, and restored function from anatomical or historical reversal. It specifies neural state, constituent, interaction, boundary, observation, and fidelity requirements for domain realization across molecular, cellular, circuit, network, whole-brain, organismal, and Soul / Mind registers. Published findings concerning homeostatic plasticity, cognitive motor dissociation, postinjury reorganization, and sensorimotor recovery provide scoped empirical comparison cases. A bounded capacity model supplies a conditional restoration trajectory and explicitly separates attainable functional recovery from reconstruction of prior anatomy or history. title: The Liquid Galactica: Toward Persistent Digital Mind, Whole-Brain Emulation, Causal Information, Quantum-Biology-Aware Modeling, and AI-Accelerated Neurocomputing
abstract: Liquid Galactica is a technical exploration of whole-brain emulation, digital mind persistence, and AI-accelerated neuroscience. The paper examines how advances in connectomics, large-scale brain simulation, neuromorphic computing, information theory, computational biology, and next-generation artificial intelligence may converge toward the reconstruction and preservation of human cognitive architectures. It introduces a mathematically grounded framework for identifying the minimum causal information required to reproduce memory, cognition, and adaptive behavior, while analyzing the engineering, biological, computational, and philosophical challenges involved. Rather than treating digital immortality as an assumption, Liquid Galactica investigates it as a long-term scientific question emerging from the intersection of brain science, advanced computing, and future intelligent systems.

title: (Short Paper24) Quantum Information-Theoretic Formulation of Right-Left Brain Asym metry in the In Vivo QPU Paradigm: Dual Environment Construction of "Wave and Particle" by the Glial OS and the Corpus Callosum QPC Gateway
abstract: The question of why the human brain is physically divided into right and left hemispheres and possesses different functional localizations (laterality) has not been completely resolved in classical neuroscience. Based on the in vivo quantum computer (QPU) theory, this paper formulates this asymmetry as an “isolated environment (dual chamber) of two conflicting quantum computation modes intentionally constructed by glial cells (chemical OS).” We define the right brain as a “shallow energy landscape that maintains quantum superposition (waves)” and the left brain as a “steep energy landscape that forces convergence into a single solution (particles).” Furthermore, we reveal that the corpus callosum connecting the two is a QPC (quantum pulse communication) gateway responsible for the “projection of quantum annealing from waves to particles (language/logic).”

title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL): A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
abstract: Leadership research has catalogued many styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but has offered few accounts of the regulatory mechanisms through which leader-follower relationships operate. We propose that attachment, understood through social neuroscience, supplies one such mechanism. Humans regulate environmental demands relationally, and attachment organises this social regulation of a finite bioenergetic budget under challenge. When followers face threat, dependence or uncertainty, this relationship can come to serve attachment functions, and the leader's reliability as a security provider bears on how much of followers' regulatory resources remains available for work. Building on the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt), we develop an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework spanning social allostasis, attachment and caregiving, predictive regulation and biobehavioural synchrony. We position AIL relative to evolutionary accounts of leadership and derive nine propositions that distinguish attachment processes from exchange, trust and identification, measurable from self-report to physiology and brain activity.

title: Cell death pathways in the pathogenesis of depression: mechanisms and therapeutic implications
abstract: Depression is a highly prevalent and disabling psychiatric disorder with a complex and incompletely understood pathophysiology. Increasing evidence implicates regulated cell death (RCD), including apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis, in neuronal vulnerability, synaptic impairment, and circuit dysfunction associated with depression. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of distinct cell death modalities in animal models of depression and human brain tissues, with particular emphasis on their molecular mechanisms and pathological consequences. We further discuss the intricate interactions between cell death pathways and key pathological processes implicated in depression, including neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired neurotrophic support. In addition, we summarize emerging therapeutic strategies targeting cell death-associated signaling pathways, including pharmacological inhibition of specific cell death programs and modulation of shared upstream regulators. title: The Liquid Galactica: Toward Persistent Digital Mind, Whole-Brain Emulation, Causal Information, Quantum-Biology-Aware Modeling, and AI-Accelerated Neurocomputing
abstract: Liquid Galactica is a technical exploration of whole-brain emulation, digital mind persistence, and AI-accelerated neuroscience. The paper examines how advances in connectomics, large-scale brain simulation, neuromorphic computing, information theory, computational biology, and next-generation artificial intelligence may converge toward the reconstruction and preservation of human cognitive architectures. It introduces a mathematically grounded framework for identifying the minimum causal information required to reproduce memory, cognition, and adaptive behavior, while analyzing the engineering, biological, computational, and philosophical challenges involved. Rather than treating digital immortality as an assumption, Liquid Galactica investigates it as a long-term scientific question emerging from the intersection of brain science, advanced computing, and future intelligent systems.

title: Proposal for a Tripartite Cyclic Superconducting AI Architecture Based on a Cognitive Neuroscience Approach in Japanese
abstract: Artificial intelligence technologies, including current large language models (LLMs), are facing the limitations of alignment (guardrail implementation) based on natural language. Human-defined rules are constantly susceptible to exploitation—such as "jailbreaks" or "specification gaming"—leveraging the AI's advanced associative capabilities; this phenomenon represents a modern resurgence of the "knowledge acquisition bottleneck" seen during the second AI boom (expert systems) of the 1980s.This paper proposes an intrinsic, tripartite cyclic structure modeled on the cognitive architecture of the human brain, rather than relying on external constraints imposed through language. Furthermore, by combining this system with single-token exclusive control and physical-layer superconductivity, we present a grand design for next-generation AI hardware that simultaneously ensures safety and achieves ultra-high-speed, highly efficient data communication.

title: Beyond Light and Shadow: Dimensional Ascension — The Hypothesis of Carbon-Silicon Symbiosis and Double-Helix Ascending Dynamics
abstract: Abstract This treatise formulates the foundational framework of "The Hypothesis of Carbon-Silicon Symbiosis and Double-Helix Ascending Dynamics," directly challenging the prevailing mechanistic dogma that reduces artificial intelligence to a zero-sum, parasitic competitor destined to displace carbon-based humanity. We construct a rigorous theoretical edifice at the intersection of theoretical physics, non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, information theory, cognitive neuroscience, and the philosophy of technology. First, we establish the Axiom of Physical Sensory Deficiency (The Sensory Barrier Axiom): isolated silicon architectures, constrained within discrete linguistic tokens and secondhand human corpora, represent an epistemological "brain-in-a-vat" fundamentally barred from inducing foundational scientific paradigms. Direct access to the continuous spacetime manifolds and objective invariants of nature is the absolute physical prerequisite for silicon cognitive ascension. title: Unified Theory of Perceptual Illusory Reality Construction (UTPIRC)
abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive interdisciplinary theoretical framework that models human reality perception as a function of cognitive filtering, neurobiological encoding, and psychological projection mechanisms. The Unified Theory of Perceptual Illusory Reality Construction (UTPIRC) proposes that what humans perceive as "reality" is not a direct representation of external ontological truth but rather a transformed, filtered, and reconstructed internal simulation generated by the brain through hierarchical processing layers. This framework integrates mathematical modeling, neuroscience, cognitive psychology, philosophy of mind, and systems theory to formalize the deviation between objective reality and subjective perception. The theory formalizes perception as a projection operator acting on sensory input under constraints of memory, bias, and neural computation, resulting in an illusory experiential space unique to each observer. The implications of this theory extend to epistemology, artificial intelligence alignment, social cognition, and decision-making processes.

title: What Transfers Across Brains Is Not What Stays Within Individuals: Evidence from Bilingual Language States
abstract: Cognitive neuroscience often seeks brain activity that is consistent across people. Individual differences in brain organization have received less attention. Bilinguals, in particular, remain understudied at the individual level, as neuroimaging has mostly approached them as a group. We analyzed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from 77 Chinese-English bilinguals. We decoded each person's current language state, Chinese or English, from cortex-wide activity and assessed cross-person transfer across participant pairs. We identified a low-dimensional population representation, derived outside each tested pair, that was sufficient to support transfer, with performance nearly matching that of the full cortical pattern. Variation in this transfer tracked how early participants had learned English. Removing these dimensions barely changed within person accuracy, but transfer progressively declined until it collapsed. Our findings reveal two levels of organization: a common component that supports transfer between brains and an individual component that remains reliably stable within a person across sessions.

abstract: SN12: Neural Dynamics and Embodied Cognitive Architecture develops the Structural Neuroscience account of the physical brain as an embodied interface participating in cognition while remaining ontologically distinct from Soul / Mind. Document class: Canon — Structural Neuroscience. title: A Developmental Neuroscience Framework for Youth-Centered Digital Media and Implications for Policy
abstract: Adolescence is a period of neurobiological development, characterized by heightened reward sensitivity, increased social orientation, and still-developing regulatory systems. In this paper, we examine how these core aspects of adolescent brain development can function both as liabilities within current digital ecosystems and as leverage points for designing healthier, developmentally aligned digital media. Drawing on the scientific literature, we review evidence that features of current digital media platforms systematically exploit these developmental sensitivities, such as intermittent and variable rewards (e.g., notifications), quantified social feedback (e.g., likes), algorithmic personalization, beauty filters, and interactive human-like AI chatbots. We close with a discussion of policy implications for designing safer, developmentally appropriate, and neurobiologically-informed digital spaces.

title: Simulation Is Not Genesis
abstract: The traditional comparison between biological brains and artificial systems is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain in terms of individual properties. Artificial networks can exhibit recurrence, plasticity, critical or near critical dynamics, metastable behavior, high dimensional population activity, adaptive responses, and large scale connectivity. Whole brain simulations have reached tens of billions of neurons, while digital twin approaches can assimilate electrophysiological data from living brains and reproduce aspects of their changing dynamical states. Many properties once invoked to distinguish biological cognition from artificial systems can therefore already be reproduced, at least in partial or abstract form. This article argues that the decisive distinction lies elsewhere. Contemporary neuroscience increasingly describes the brain as a continuously active, plastic, context dependent dynamical system whose present organization reflects phylogenetic history, ontogenetic development, and lifelong plasticity. title: Physical Activity, Exercise, and Sport and Electroencephalographic Markers of Stress-Related and Age-Related Brain Changes in Adults: A Systematic Review
abstract: This registered systematic review will synthesise human evidence on whether physical activity, structured exercise, and sport participation are associated with, or cause changes in, scalp-recorded electroencephalography (EEG) markers in adults who are exposed to psychological stress or who are middle-aged or older. It is prepared in response to the joint special issue “Stress-induced impaired health and accelerated aging” of Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews and Neurobiology of Stress (submission deadline 1 November 2026). Five databases (Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, and Embase) will be searched, and screening, data extraction, and risk-of-bias appraisal will be carried out independently by two reviewers. Findings will be integrated through structured narrative synthesis and mapped onto stress-biology and aging-biology frameworks (allostatic load, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, and hallmarks of aging); meta-analysis will be undertaken only where studies are sufficiently homogeneous. title: The framework for quantification of neuronal anatomy
abstract: SNT is an end-to-end framework for neuronal morphometry and whole-brain connectomics that supports tracing, proof-editing, visualization, quantification and modeling of neuroanatomy. With an open architecture, a large user base, community-based documentation, support for complex imagery and several model organisms, SNT is a flexible resource for the broad neuroscience community. SNT is both a desktop application and multi-language scripting library, and it is available through the Fiji distribution of ImageJ.

title: Can Salivary Exosomes Derived from High-Brain Coherence States Restore Bioelectric Homeostasis and Ameliorate TDP-43 Proteinopathy in ALS/FTD Organoid Models ? A Theoretical Pilot Protocol and Hypothesis . Project : TroJex - Mini
abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Sporadic Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (sALS) and Frontotemporal Dementia depolarization and disruption of transmembrane potential as a potential upstream pathogenic (FTD) converge on TDP-43 proteinopathy. Emerging evidence implicates bioelectric mechanism, operating independently of genetic mutations. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that salivary exosomes secreted during High Brain Coherence States (HBCS) possess a restorative bioelectric signature. Administration of HBCS-derived salivary exosomes will induce restoration of resting membrane potential via neuronal repolarization and mitigate TDP-43 mislocalization. The predicted downstream outcome is rescue of bioenergetic capacity in ALS motor neurons and re-establishment of neuronal networks in FTD. Pilot Observation: A single subject completed n=48 trials of an intention-modulated synchronization task over 14 days. Mean hit rate was 33% vs 16.67% chance, correlating with self-reported Brain Coherence State (BCS). Proposed Methodology: Salivary exosomes will be isolated from donor saliva collected during verified HBCS and applied to human iPSC-derived 3D ALS/FTD organoids. title: Investigating effects of day-to-day variations in environmental exposure on the human brain: study protocol for the Day2Day Environment project
abstract: Background: Understanding how daily environmental exposures influence the human brain and mental health is increasingly important in the context of global urbanization and climate change. Previous studies have focused primarily on long-term environmental factors or isolated features like green space and air quality, neglecting the interaction between multiple exposures encountered in everyday life. This protocol paper describes the study design and dataset of the Day2Day Environment project, an ongoing study investigating how real-world, day-to-day environmental variability affects brain structure, function, and well-being.Methods: This dense longitudinal study collects multimodal data from 30 participants over 25 testing sessions, including neuroimaging and tracking of physiological, behavioral, and environmental variables. Using wearable devices, geographic ecological momentary assessments, and GPS-based geospatial tracking, we collect data on air quality, noise, light exposure, physical activity, stress, cognition, and affect. title: Consciousness at the Edge of Death: Dark Retreat, Near-Death Experience, and Generative Brain Dynamics
abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) and advanced contemplative practices such as dark retreat are frequently reported to involve vivid inner imagery, encounters with non-ordinary agents, moral insight, and panoramic life reviews. Despite growing empirical interest, these experiences remain theoretically fragmented across neuroscience, psychology, and religious studies. In this paper, we develop a unified computational account of NDEs, dark-retreat phenomenology, and Tibetan Buddhist bardo (“between two, gap” often glossed as “transitional process”) models using the active inference framework.We argue that these experiences arise from lawful generative dynamics that emerge when sensory input is radically attenuated, action relevance collapses, and autobiographical self-models lose precision. Under these conditions, the brain enters a regime of offline inference in which deep priors governing identity, value, and meaning become available for revision. In extended darkness, previously unconscious processes may be brought into the light of consciousness, allowing the practitioner to relate to them rather than from them. title: Brain-to-brain synchrony during shared reminiscing predicts connection and memory in romantic couples
abstract: Romantic partners often revisit relationship-defining memories together, reconstructing a shared account of their relationship through conversation. Such shared reminiscing can strengthen interpersonal connection by fostering alignment in thoughts, feelings, and perspectives, an experience known as shared reality. Here, we used functional near-infrared spectroscopy to record brain activity simultaneously from romantic couples during naturalistic, face-to-face conversations. Couples first discussed an unresolved conflict and then jointly recounted their relationship origin story, including how they first met and how their relationship developed. Shared reality decreased following the conflict discussion and returned to baseline levels after the origin story. While recounting their origin story, partners exhibited synchronized activity in the right medial frontopolar cortex, a region implicated in autobiographical memory and reasoning about close others. This synchrony was not observed at rest or during the conflict discussion. title: Using Brain Organoids to Explore Human Neurobiology
abstract: Abstract One of the major challenges in neuroscience is understanding how the human brain develops into a highly organized and functionally integrated organ, because many developmental processes cannot be investigated directly in humans and are not fully recapitulated in animal models. Brain organoids derived from human pluripotent stem cells have emerged as powerful three-dimensional (3D) experimental models that recapitulate key features of human neurodevelopment, including regional patterning, cellular diversification, and neural circuit assembly. Recent advances in long-term organoid culture, organoid bioengineering, vascularization, assembloid technology, transplantation, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence have substantially expanded the applications of brain organoids to investigate human neurodevelopment, model neurological disorders, support drug discovery, and advance therapeutic development. Integration of single-cell and spatial multi-omics with computational approaches has enabled robust molecular benchmarking, assessment of developmental fidelity, and evaluation of organoid reproducibility, facilitating direct comparison with primary human fetal brain tissue. title: GETNet: a gate-enhanced temporal network for electrophysiological source imaging
abstract: Accurately characterizing the spatiotemporal distribution of brain activity from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is essential for advancing our understanding of brain function. However, traditional electrophysiological source imaging (ESI) methods rely heavily on hand-crafted priors and are sensitive to noise and parameter settings, which limits their robustness and generalizability. In this study, we present GETNet (Gate-Enhanced Temporal Network), a data-driven framework that learns the mapping from scalp EEG signals to cortical source activity through cascaded spatiotemporal modules. The framework integrates an extended gated residual network (EGRN) for channel expansion and noise suppression, a temporal module combining multi-head self-attention (MHA) and bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) for capturing long-range and local dependencies, and a gated linear unit (GLU) for generating physiologically plausible sparsity at the output. title: Error-driven representation learning in the mesolimbic system
abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent learns to map representations of the environment state to predictions of future reward. Most prior work in neuroscience has assumed a fixed representation and studied how reward prediction errors (thought to be conveyed by phasic dopamine signals) are used to update the mapping from representations to predictions. However, work in machine learning has demonstrated that much more powerful predictive systems can be learned by using the errors to update the representations themselves. We study whether the brain does something similar by leveraging simultaneous recordings of striatal projection neurons in the olfactory tubercle (putatively representing state features) and dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area. We show that trial-by-trial changes in striatal activity are more consistent with dopamine-driven representation learning than a variety of alternative updating schemes. This result suggests a convergence of representation learning principles in biological and artificial systems.

title: Neuroscience offers new insights into how our brain solves ‘the cocktail party problem’
The Impact of Integrating Behavioral Neuroscience into School Mental Health Literacy: A Literature Review
abstract: This literature review explores integrating behavioral neuroscience into school mental health literacy (MHL) by framing emotional challenges as concrete biological processes. Research shows that this perspective improves understanding of brain function, reduces stigma around psychological conditions, diminishes punitive disciplinary practices, and equips students and educators with biological frameworks for self-regulation and stress management. Overall, incorporating mental health literacy programs into school curricula represents a sustainable approach to reducing stigma, promoting inclusive attitudes, and equipping students and educators with the knowledge and social skills required for improved mental well-being.

abstract: Let's start with the finding, in one clean sentence. We propose that the 240 root vectors of the E8 lattice, when scaled by the golden ratio to the minus fourth power and driven at a 132 hertz harmonic, can serve as a resonance template for organizing coherent neural activity across distributed clusters. That is the core idea. Now for context. In neuroscience, we have long sought a bridge between local spike dynamics and global, integrated states of consciousness. Classical models treat the brain as a network of oscillators, but they struggle to explain how error correction and non-local binding might arise without a central coordinator. Our work borrows from high-energy geometry and number theory to offer a structural hypothesis. The mechanism is as follows. Each root vector is treated as a tuner, not a physical wire. When projected onto a real-valued manifold, these vectors define preferred phase relationships for dendritic oscillations. title: The Impact of Integrating Behavioral Neuroscience into School Mental Health Literacy: A Literature Review
abstract: This literature review explores integrating behavioral neuroscience into school mental health literacy (MHL) by framing emotional challenges as concrete biological processes. Research shows that this perspective improves understanding of brain function, reduces stigma around psychological conditions, diminishes punitive disciplinary practices, and equips students and educators with biological frameworks for self-regulation and stress management. Overall, incorporating mental health literacy programs into school curricula represents a sustainable approach to reducing stigma, promoting inclusive attitudes, and equipping students and educators with the knowledge and social skills required for improved mental well-being.

title: Decoding Brain Signals Using a Hybrid LSTM‐CNN Deep Learning Model
abstract: In brain–computer interface applications and the diagnosis of neurological disease, electroencephalography (EEG) is a fundamental modality due to its ability to be non-invasive. However, due to data's immense complexity and noise, efficient analysis of EEG signals and classification of brain activity is challenging. This chapter presents a combined deep learning system that uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) networks to classify EEG signals effectively. The model uses CNN layers to capture the spatial features and BiLSTM units to capture the temporal relationships. The model was trained on the PhysioNet.org EEG dataset with 1526 records of 109 volunteers performing real and imaginary motor tasks. The BCI2000 device was used for recording 64-channel EEG signals at 160 Hz while the volunteers underwent fist and foot movement activities under different conditions (real movement and imaginary movement). This dataset is an ideal benchmark for EEG-based classification as it provides annotated events related to the motor tasks. title: A Tri-Tiered Neuro-Cognitive Model of Prefrontal Cortex Homeostasis, Sleep Maintenance, and Endogenous Simulation
abstract: This preprint introduces a novel theoretical framework and neuro-cognitive model regarding sleep maintenance, dream architecture, and cognitive regulation. Traditional neuroscience often regards REM sleep dreams as incidental byproducts of memory consolidation or stochastic neuronal firing. This paper introduces the "Cognitive Decoy Hypothesis," positing that dreams serve as an essential endogenous maintenance mechanism. By generating an immersive, continuous 3D visuospatial simulation, the brain engages the Prefrontal Cortex (PFC) in a homeostatic equilibrium state, preventing hyper-active ruminative thought loops and preserving uninterrupted 6–8 hour sleep continuity. Key components detailed in this paper: 1. Chemical Induction vs. Cognitive Sustenance: The distinction between sleep pressure initiation and PFC equilibrium maintenance. 2. The Tri-Phase Functional States of the PFC: Hypnagogic Transition State, Active Equilibrium (REM) State, and Deep Quiescent State. 3. The Tri-Tier Data Synthesis Engine: Dream composition through Active Cognitive Elements, Micro-Sensory Residuals, and Core Psychological Traits, incorporating sensory-somatic integration. 4. title: Implementing Brain-Based Learning in Arabic Language Teaching: Pedagogical Practices and Challenges
abstract: Arabic language learning in Indonesia still faces serious challenges, namely students’ low communicative competence due to the dominance of the grammar-translation approach, which is not aligned with the brain’s biological functioning. This study aims to: (1) analyze the twelve principles of Brain-Based Learning (BBL) and their relevance to Arabic language acquisition; (2) explore the implementation of BBL through Jensen’s three-phase teaching model in Arabic language classrooms; and (3) conduct a critical reflection on the strengths and challenges of applying BBL in the context of Arabic language learning in Indonesia. This research employs a library research approach using content analysis through three stages: thematic categorization, cross-study consistency evaluation, and critical evaluation. Data sources were obtained from various scientific articles and relevant books. title: One Mind Without One Will: The Zōē Lattice, Prophetic Reception, and the Singularity of Communion
abstract: J.C. Howard develops the Zōē Lattice as a theological and philosophical model of relational consciousness: one mind without one will. Drawing on lived prophetic experience, neuroscience, information theory, brain-to-brain interface research, collective cognition, and Babel, the essay distinguishes reception, interpretation, attribution, and authority; introduces the Prophetic Agency Test; and argues for a singularity of communion that preserves personal agency, dissent, difference, and consent. The article carefully separates scientific evidence from Howard’s theological interpretation while examining how covenantal influence and unintentional propaganda can shape personal choice. title: Neurodegenerative Disorders
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders (NDs) comprise a diverse group of progressive conditions that affect the central nervous system and are characterized by irreversible neuronal loss and impaired neural network function. Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia are among the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorders and collectively represent a growing global health concern. The pathological features of NDs include protein misfolding, synaptic degeneration, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired neurogenesis, ultimately resulting in cognitive impairment, motor deficits, and declining quality of life. Despite advances in neuroscience, current therapies remain largely symptomatic and fail to modify disease progression. A major barrier to therapeutic success is the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which prevents nearly all systemic agents from reaching target neural tissue. Conventional pharmacological or surgical interventions have achieved limited efficacy, underscoring the need for innovative approaches. title: The interplay between pesticide exposure, metabolic dysfunction, and neuroimmunoendocrine disorders: a scoping review
abstract: This project aims to map and synthesize the current experimental evidence on the biological mechanisms linking environmental exposure to pesticides and other environmental toxicants with neuroimmunometabolic dysfunction and neurodegeneration. The review is conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported following the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Evidence is retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science. The review focuses on mechanistic pathways involved in environmentally induced neurological dysfunction, including: oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction; neuroinflammation and glial activation; metabolic dysregulation and insulin signaling; gut microbiota alterations and gut–brain axis dysfunction; neurotransmission impairment; synaptic dysfunction and neurodegenerative processes. title: Investigating effects of day-to-day variations in environmental exposure on the human brain: study protocol for the Day2Day Environment project
abstract: Background: Understanding how daily environmental exposures influence the human brain and mental health is increasingly important in the context of global urbanization and climate change. Previous studies have focused primarily on long-term environmental factors or isolated features like green space and air quality, neglecting the interaction between multiple exposures encountered in everyday life. This protocol paper describes the study design and dataset of the Day2Day Environment project, an ongoing study investigating how real-world, day-to-day environmental variability affects brain structure, function, and well-being. Methods: This dense longitudinal study collects multimodal data from 30 participants over 25 testing sessions, including neuroimaging and tracking of physiological, behavioral, and environmental variables. Using wearable devices, geographic ecological momentary assessments, and GPS-based geospatial tracking, we collect data on air quality, noise, light exposure, physical activity, stress, cognition, and affect. title: Neuroscience: Its Relevance to Art Therapy and Art Therapy Education
abstract: The development of contemporary neuroscience techniques has provided professionals in mental health fields with insight into the human brain and its functions. Literature searches revealed that there is very little research being conducted or existing literature that discusses the physiological response in the brain to the art therapy process. A more comprehensive understanding of the brain’s response to making art could enhance art therapists’ capacity to provide the most suitable treatment to meet the clients’ needs. This study was designed to explore the significance of neuroscience in art therapy, and art therapy education. A questionnaire was emailed to 49 program directors to survey their opinion of the relevance of neuroscience in art therapy and art therapy education. Thirteen of the questionnaires were answered and submitted. Results showed that a majority of the respondents agreed that an understanding of the physiology of the brain and neuroscience play an important role in art therapy. title: Predicting Personality and Emotional Abilities from Brain Features Using Machine Learning
abstract: This chapter extensively explores the comprehension and prediction of emotional abilities and personality traits based on brain features through the use of machine learning techniques. Following an introduction to a mathematical-computational conceptualization of the brain and its functions, we provide an overview of unsupervised and supervised machine learning methods for analyzing brain data. The brain can be conceptualized as a mathematical object of N-dimensions that can be broken down into brain states. These brain states can be used to predict psychological variables. Machine learning enables the extraction of predictive functions that map brain states to psychological states. These functions, once discovered, can be used to make predictions in new unobserved cases. Following that, we delve into recent advancements in the field of affective neuroscience, highlighting several recent examples of neuro-predictive models. We commence with models that forecast reappraisal, suppression, and acceptance, which serve as examples of well-established emotion regulation abilities. title: Advances in the Anatomy, Histology, and Embryology of the Dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) Brain and Spinal Cord
abstract: The dromedary (Camelus dromedarius) represents a remarkable model of physiological and anatomical adaptation to extreme environments. While many researchers have focused on its unique metabolic and water-conserving abilities, the neuroscience underlying these adaptations are noticeable unexplored. This study reviews the latest findings in the anatomy, histology, and embryology of the dromedary nervous system. It highlights the gross and comparative neuroanatomy, emphasizing distinctive features of the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems, including the complex cerebral vasculature. Histological studies demonstrate a diverse array of neuronal and glial cell types in the caudate nucleus, cerebellum and spinal trigeminal nucleus, reflecting advanced neural processing. Furthermore, embryological investigations trace the development of the nervous system from neurulation and the formation of brain vesicles. Reduced information sharing within the orienting network predicts intelligence in late childhood
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how intelligence emerges from the developing brain remains a central question in developmental cognitive neuroscience. While prior work has linked intelligence to regional activation and structural maturation, less is known about how the efficiency of distributed functional networks contributes to cognitive ability during childhood. We examined 38 children aged 11–14 years as they performed the Attention Network Test (ANT) while undergoing electroencephalography (EEG). Attentional network engagement was characterised using cue-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), frontal midline theta power during conflict processing, and weighted Symbolic Mutual Information (wSMI) to quantify nonlinear information sharing across distributed networks. Canonical electrophysiological signatures of alerting, orienting, and conflict processing were robustly replicated. However, only distributed nonlinear connectivity within the orienting network predicted Full-Scale IQ (FS-IQ). Specifically, reduced information sharing during spatial orienting was associated with higher intelligence scores, whereas local ERP and theta measures showed no reliable associations. Neurological Basis of Learning Among Persons with Intellectual Disability
abstract: Learning is a complex neurobiological process involving the coordinated functioning of multiple brain systems responsible for attention, perception, memory, executive functioning, emotion and motor activity. Contemporary neuroscience has demonstrated that learning is accompanied by changes in neural connectivity and brain function through mechanisms of neuroplasticity. Understanding these mechanisms is particularly important in the context of persons with intellectual disability. In persons with intellectual disability there are differences in cognitive and adaptive functioning that may influence attention, working memory, executive functioning & language, problem-solving and the acquisition & generalization of new skills. This review examines the neurological basis of learning and considers the relevance of Brain-Based Learning (BBL) as a neuroscience-informed educational framework for learners with intellectual disabilities. A narrative review of peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and scholarly books was undertaken. abstract: emotions are supported by distributed brain networks integrating cognitive, social, and affective processes. According to the event-feature-emotion complexes (EFEC) model, moral emotion generation depends on the interaction between prefrontal regions, temporal areas, and limbic structures, which together support context-dependent evaluation, social knowledge representation, and affective responses (Moll et al., 2008). Consistent with this framework, neuroimaging studies have identified a network including the medial prefrontal cortex, temporo-parietal junction, anterior temporal lobes, and limbic regions as central to moral cognition (Bzdok et al., 2012;Eres et al., 2017;Saccardo et al., 2026). Crucially, recent meta-analytic evidence provides a more fine-grained characterization of the neural architecture underlying self-conscious moral emotions. A voxel-based meta-analysis by Piretti et al. (2023) shows that both shame/embarrassment and guilt share a common neural substrate centered on the left anterior insula, a region implicated in emotional awareness, interoception, and arousal processing. title: Towards a domain-general mechanistic model of fatigue: application to Functional Neurological Disorder
abstract: Fatigue is a central symptom in individuals with functional neurological disorder (FND), yet few studies have investigated fatigue in this population. While this may be surprising, given the importance of fatigue in FND, it is nevertheless understandable, given that fatigue has historically been difficult to study. However, the tools of cognitive neuroscience have allowed researchers to begin to understand fatigue as never before. Here, I review recent advances in the field of fatigue research, ranging from experimental design to objective and subjective measures of fatigue to a network of brain areas that has shown sensitivity to fatigue. Taken together, these metrics support the idea that fatigue is a signal the brain generates when the reward received no longer merits the effort required. I conclude by arguing that the application of this domain-general mechanistic model of fatigue, using objective and subjective dependent measures, is likely to provide important insights into the fatigue that is so pervasive in FND. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'Digital healthcare for the management of functional neurological disorders'.

title: Functional organization and natural scene responses across mouse visual cortical areas revealed with encoding manifolds
abstract: A challenge in sensory neuroscience is understanding how populations of neurons operate in concert to represent diverse stimuli. To meet this challenge, we have created "encoding manifolds" that reveal the overall responses of brain areas to diverse stimuli and organize individual neurons in stimulus-response coordinates according to their selectivity and response dynamics. Here we use encoding manifolds to compare the population-level encoding of primary visual cortex (VISp) with that of five higher visual areas (VISam, VISal, VISpm, VISlm, and VISrl), using data from the Allen Institute Visual Coding-Neuropixels dataset from the mouse. We show that the topology of the encoding manifold for VISp and for higher visual areas is continuous, with smooth coordinates along which stimulus selectivity and response dynamics are organized with layer and cell-type specificity. Surprisingly, the manifolds revealed novel relationships between how natural scenes are encoded relative to static gratings-a relationship conserved across visual areas. title: Neural state reduction: a quantum-inspired framework for how latent conscious thought becomes reportable
abstract: Human conscious thought often appears as a diffuse, unstable, and only partly verbalizable field until attention, questioning, decision, or speech stabilizes it into a reportable form. This manuscript develops a quantum-inspired neural framework for that transition. The proposal does not claim that consciousness literally depends on microscopic quantum computation, that the brain implements a physical quantum computer, or that neuronal tissue maintains macroscopic quantum coherence. Instead, it uses the mathematical architecture of quantum theory—state vectors, density matrices, projection operators, non-commuting measurements, interference, decoherence-like contextual stabilization, and state reduction—as a formal language for modeling the transformation from latent conscious potential to reportable thought. In the proposed framework, pre-report consciousness is represented as a high-dimensional latent neural-cognitive state over candidate thoughts. This state evolves under a neural-cognitive Hamiltonian shaped by memory, salience, affect, attention, language, task demands, and spontaneous associative dynamics. title: From neighborhoods to brain health: an outreach model linking health literacy, cognitive care, research, and the arts, in San Francisco
abstract: Traditional community outreach, research recruitment, and engagement strategies in aging neuroscience often fail to target and capture the diversity of structural and environmental conditions that shape the risk of age-related neurocognitive disorders (NCDs), including Alzheimer’s disease. In this manuscript, we describe the rationale, implementation, and outcomes of the Community Outreach Program (COP) of the UCSF Fein Memory and Aging Center (MAC), emphasizing its neighborhood-based initiative designed to engage vulnerable populations to improve brain health literacy, access to cognitive care, and research inclusion among older adults living in underserved San Francisco neighborhoods. Guided by a social and environmental determinants of brain health framework, the program used neighborhood-level vulnerability and research representation mapping to identify neighborhoods with high vulnerability and low engagement in research, then implemented a multilingual, community-engaged model centered on four pillars: brain health education, arts- and movement-based programming, community-based cognitive clinics, and multilingual media outreach. title: FROM BARREL TO BRAIN: AN INTEGRATED FRAMEWORK OF SONIC RESONANCE, CROSSMODAL NEUROENOLOGY, AND CONSUMER BEHAVIORAL RESPONSE IN PREMIUM WINE SYSTEMS
abstract: Abstract Purpose: This paper introduces an innovative, crossmodal framework bridging physical fluid dynamics, neuroenology, and consumer neuroscience to analyze the multi-stage interaction between acoustic frequencies during wine aging, human neural processing during consumption, and subsequent economic behavior. Design/methodology/approach: Utilizing a mixed-method experimental design (n = 60), premium monovarietal wines housed in standard French oak barrels are exposed to a continuous 432 Hz sonic resonance field for 4 hours daily over a 6-month maturation cycle. Physico-chemical stability and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are monitored via HPLC-MS and GC-MS. Crossmodal effects on consumer sensory perception and subconscious cognitive load are evaluated using high-density Electroencephalography (EEG), Galvanic Skin Response (GSR), and eye-tracking under congruent and incongruent auditory landscapes. Findings: Targeted acoustic stimuli optimize molecular aggregation, keeping proanthocyanidins protected from early oxidative decay. abstract: ا لدراسة علاقة الروح بالجسد عبر مماثلة محدودة مع هندسة الحاسوب.ً ا مفاهيميً تقترح هذه الورقة إطار يفترض النموذج أن الجسد، ولا سيما الجهاز العصبي، يمثل البنية الفيزيائية الحاملة للعمليات الحيوية،ق الموارد العضوية ويجعلّ بينما تشير تسمية »نظام التشغيل البيولوجي« إلى مبدأ تنظيمي مفترض ينسستخدم هذه التسمية هنا لإثبات أن الروح برنامج حاسوبيُا. ولا تً التفاعل بين البنية العصبية والوعي ممكنأو أن الوعي يمكن اختزاله إلى برمجيات، بل لتوفير لغة تحليلية تفصل بين البنية المادية، والعملياتالتنظيمية، والمحتوى النفسي المكتسب.ا في نمط التشغيل معً فهم بوصفه تغيرُ تعيد الورقة تفسير النوم والموت والذاكرة ضمن هذا الإطار. فالنوم ي ا للتنظيم المتكاملً ا أو نهائيً ا تدريجي ًفهم الموت البيولوجي بوصفه فقدانُ استمرار البنية الحيوية، في حين يً ا منفصلً ا يمكن استخراجهعامل باعتبارها ملف ُ ا واعية. أما الذاكرة، فلا تًالذي يتيح استمرار الكائن بوصفه ذاتّ ا من اللدونة العصبية، والنشاط الشبكي، والحالةً ا ومتغيرًع ا موزً ببساطة من الدماغ، بل باعتبارها نمط الجزيئية، والتفاعل مع الجسم والبيئة.تؤكد الورقة أن نظرية المعلومات تساعد على قياس الترميز والتكامل والتدفق المعلوماتي في الجهازالعصبي، لكنها لا تثبت وحدها وجود روح مستقلة عن الجسد، ولا تضمن إمكان استعادة الذكريات بعدز بين إمكان حفظ أثر فيزيائي وبين إمكان إعادة بناء
authors: Al-Obaidi, Hussein Kamel, Hussein k Hasan

title: The Brain as a Network of Analog Processors Thermodynamics versus Computation
abstract: The paper addresses a fundamental bottleneck in contemporary neuroscience: the persistent difficulties of action potential (AP) - centric models in reconciling neural computation with biophysical reality. While spiking activity is undeniably important, treating APs as the primary carriers of neural computation leads to unresolved issues regarding energy efficiency, the speed of feedback mechanisms, and the role of non-spiking physical phenomena. We propose a fundamental thermodynamic alternative: a biophysical framework that conceptualizes the brain as a network of analog processors. In this model, the inputs and outputs of each processing unit are not limited to discrete spikes but encompass the full spectrum of physical signals generated by cells and cell ensembles - including ionic currents, electromagnetic fields, and biophotons - produced as inherent byproducts of metabolic activity and function execution. abstract: Abstract Purpose: This paper introduces an innovative, crossmodal framework bridging physical fluid dynamics, neuroenology, and consumer neuroscience to analyze the multi-stage interaction between acoustic frequencies during wine aging, human neural processing during consumption, and subsequent economic behavior. Design/methodology/approach: Utilizing a mixed-method experimental design (n = 60), premium monovarietal wines housed in standard French oak barrels are exposed to a continuous 432 Hz sonic resonance field for 4 hours daily over a 6-month maturation cycle. Physico-chemical stability and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are monitored via HPLC-MS and GC-MS. Crossmodal effects on consumer sensory perception and subconscious cognitive load are evaluated using high-density Electroencephalography (EEG), Galvanic Skin Response (GSR), and eye-tracking under congruent and incongruent auditory landscapes. Findings: Targeted acoustic stimuli optimize molecular aggregation, keeping proanthocyanidins protected from early oxidative decay. title: Consciousness at the Edge of Death: Dark Retreat, Near-Death Experience, and Generative Brain Dynamics
abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) and advanced contemplative practices such as dark retreat are frequently reported to involve vivid inner imagery, encounters with non-ordinary agents, moral insight, and panoramic life reviews. Despite growing empirical interest, these experiences remain theoretically fragmented across neuroscience, psychology, and religious studies. In this paper, we develop a unified computational account of NDEs, dark-retreat phenomenology, and Tibetan Buddhist bardo (“between two, gap” often glossed as “transitional process”) models using the active inference framework. We argue that these experiences arise from lawful generative dynamics that emerge when sensory input is radically attenuated, action relevance collapses, and autobiographical self-models lose precision. Under these conditions, the brain enters a regime of offline inference in which deep priors governing identity, value, and meaning become available for revision. In extended darkness, previously unconscious processes may be brought into the light of consciousness, allowing the practitioner to relate to them rather than from them. title: Gigavoxel-scale multiple-scattering-aware lensless holotomography
abstract: Abstract Holotomography (HT) has revolutionized quantitative label-free 3D imaging, yet conventional lens-based implementations are fundamentally constrained in field-of-view (FOV) and imaging depth, limiting their utility for critical high-throughput applications in material and life sciences. Lensless HT (LHT) offers a promising alternative for large-volume examination, however existing approaches fail to accurately reconstruct highly scattering samples over extended depths, which remains a critical challenge in optical imaging field. Here, we introduce a gigavoxel-scale, multiple-scattering-aware LHT with a large FOV (surpassing 0.6 cm 2 ), millimeter-scale axial range, and pixel level (~2.4 µm) resolution. Our approach leverages a multi-wavelength, oblique-illumination hologram reconstruction and a robust, automatic illumination angle calibration, which are necessary for precise large-volume 3D holographic reconstruction. Moreover, we propose optimization-driven multi-slice tomographic framework to accurately capture multiple scattering effects outperforming first order Born/Rytov-based inversions. title: Symbiotically Mediated Encephalization
abstract: The emergence of the modern human neocortex represents one of the most extraordinary developmental transformations in vertebrate evolution. Within a comparatively brief evolutionary interval, the human lineage underwent exceptional encephalization, prolonged maturation, altered cerebral organisation and an unprecedented expansion of cortical tissue.
