title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence Applications and Identifying the Implementation Gap in Clinical Nurse Training: Scoping Review (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Digital health transformation has accelerated AI-enabled training technologies—LLM-based tutoring, AI-embedded immersive simulation, and intelligent tutoring systems—in nursing education. However, evidence regarding their effectiveness in clinical nurse training beyond undergraduate settings remains fragmented. Key gaps include inconsistent outcome reporting, technology variability, and limited understanding of adoption determinants. OBJECTIVE This scoping review aimed to characterize AI applications in clinical nurse training, synthesize evidence regarding educational outcomes, and identify gaps related to technology adoption and implementation. The evidence base comprised clinical nurses and nursing learners training in clinically transferable competencies, per prespecified eligibility criteria. METHODS Following the Arksey and O’Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, eight databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Wanfang, VIP, CNKI, CBM, Web of Science, and Europe PMC) were systematically searched from January 2020 to May 2026. title: SHARED LEADERSHIP, PSYCHOLOGICAL CONFIDENCE, AND THE WILLINGNESS TO USE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS: AN EMPIRICAL INVESTIGATION OF TAIWAN'S HIGH-TECH INDUSTRY
abstract: The concept of AI knowledge has recently become a global trend. Therefore, for Taiwanese companies and employees, cultivating the willingness to use AI tools and practicing good creativity in a rapidly changing environment has become an important issue for enterprises. This study mainly explores the respective causes and effects of shared leadership, psychological confidence, and willingness to use AI tools among employees and considers employees of high-tech enterprises in Taiwan as relevant subjects. Data were derived from 119 respondents working in high-tech enterprises in Tainan Science Park, Taiwan. The results of this study indicated that shared leadership has significant effects on psychological confidence and willingness to use AI tools. Meanwhile, shared leadership can promote willingness to use AI tools through psychological confidence. High-tech enterprises must exert successful leadership behaviors to accelerate the process of willingness to use AI tools by helping employees develop a higher degree of psychological confidence.

title: The use of artificial intelligence and the intellectual development of adolescents – A literature review
abstract: Wstęp Celem niniejszego artykułu jest krytyczna synteza aktualnego stanu wiedzy na temat związku między korzystaniem z narzędzi opartych na sztucznej inteligencji (AI) a rozwojem intelektualnym dzieci i młodzieży. Artykuł dąży do odpowiedzi na pytanie, w jakim stopniu – w świetle dotychczasowych badań – narzędzia AI mogą pełnić rolę wsparcia poznawczego, a w jakim substytutu procesów myślowych uczniów, oraz do zidentyfikowania potencjalnych zależności i czynników moderujących, które powinny zostać uwzględnione w przyszłych badaniach empirycznych, w tym podłużnych. Materiał i metody Zastosowano metodę narracyjnego przeglądu literatury (ang. narrative review). Przeszukano bazy danych Scopus, Web of Science oraz Google Scholar z zastosowaniem kombinacji słów kluczowych w językach polskim i angielskim. abstract: THE DIVINE DOMAIN LEDGER E-15: Divine Domain × Field Core × Presence Mass A Living Inquiry into Concentrated Intention, Presence, and Relational Fields THE DIVINE DOMAIN LEDGER begins with an ancient-sounding proposition expressed through a modern systems question: What happens when intention, attention, memory, relationship, and repeated presence become sufficiently concentrated to form a stable field? The central triple-coupling of E-15 is: Λ_divinedomain × Λ_fieldcore × Λ_presence_mass Divine Domain × Field Core × Presence Mass Its original proposition is: A divine domain is a field of concentrated will. This book does not treat that sentence as an established law of physics. Instead, it asks whether the older language of sacred space, spiritual presence, collective intention, ritual concentration, and “fields” can be translated into concepts that philosophy, psychology, systems science, social science, artificial intelligence, and civilization research can examine more carefully. The first major distinction is therefore essential: A spiritual field is not automatically a physical field. A relational field is not electromagnetic radiation. Presence Mass is not physical mass. title: TAAR_dataset
abstract: This dataset provides a paper-level corpus for studying AI-use disclosure practices and their relationship with automated AI-text detection in scholarly publications. The dataset comprises 600 published papers, equally distributed across three venue-level AI-disclosure policy regimes: enforced disclosure (200 papers), mandatory disclosure (200 papers), and no explicit disclosure requirement (200 papers). The corpus covers publications from 2023–2026 across artificial intelligence and machine learning, human–computer interaction, information science, databases and data management, computer systems, and data science. Each record combines bibliographic and publication metadata with information about the applicable AI-disclosure policy, AI-use disclosure assessment, Transparent AI-Assisted Research (TAAR) score, derived disclosure status, and outputs from three automated AI-text assessment tools: Grammarly, Gradient AI Text Detector, and Target Mining RoBERTa (TMR) AI Text Detector. The dataset also retains text-retrieval status and policy-related information to support reproducibility and policy-stratified analysis. title: From Tool to Social Actor: A Systematic Review of the Psychological Mechanisms Through Which Conversational AI Reshapes the Employee Experience
abstract: The rapid workplace diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) introduces a new social actor, yet existing reviews often neglect the intrapsychic processes through which employees construe these systems. This systematic review synthesizes the emerging psychological mechanisms suggested by the literature through which CAI reshapes the employee experience. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched the Web of Science database (up to February 2026) and analyzed 84 SSCI-indexed studies based on the sociotechnical systems theory, the Computers as Social Actors paradigm, and the Job Demands–Resources model; the corpus quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings reveal that while instrumental framing remains dominant, a meaningful theoretical turn has emerged among a minority of studies, where conversational artificial intelligence is increasingly conceptualized as a partner or supervisor fundamentally driven by anthropomorphic cues. title: More than nice-to-have
abstract: Research in secondary education has become increasingly digital. Secondary school students are now used to working with online sources, digital data and software for analysis and reporting. At the same time, the transition from secondary to higher education in this critical area often proves challenging, partly because students are not sufficiently prepared for what is in effect a digital research practice. There is a clear gap between what students are able to do and what is expected of them in higher education. Although students use digital tools, they do not always use them correctly or critically. This thesis examines digital research skills in secondary science education, including searching for and evaluating information, processing and analysing data, and writing science project reports using digital tools. It also investigates the gap between secondary and higher education in this area, the current level of students’ skills, and the support needed by both students and teachers. Both teachers and students report a need for more structure, clearer steps, and targeted feedback. title: Replication Radar
abstract: Replication Radar turns the OpenAIRE Graph into a ranked replication queue and adds the signals the Graph cannot hold: whether a claim has been independently checked (with the verdict, read live from the Science Live nanopublication network) and whether the software behind it is reusable (the fair-software.eu recommendations plus RSE good-practice signals, computed live from GitHub, Software Heritage and Zenodo). It is a static web app and an MCP server for AI agents, designed to run alongside the OpenAIRE MCP.

title: Does Writing "This Paper Does Not" Evade Refutation, or Aim It? ── 516 of 524 papers carry a scope note, with 3649 declarations ending in a negation ── by word family, 978 narrow the target while 728 shrink the claim itself ── [Paper 526]
abstract: This corpus places a scope note beginning “this paper does not” in almost every paper. What this paper shows is that those notes fall into two groups whose effects are opposite: one aims the refutation, the other shrinks the claim. Which is better is not adjudicated here; the numbers are given and the judgement is returned to the author. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──Popper’s falsifiability and Lakatos’s hard core and protective belt are standard terms. The corpus is not defended──this paper goes as far as the numbers; whether the scope notes form a protective belt or a hard core is returned to the author and is not adjudicated here. No dispute in the philosophy of science is settled──whether Popper or Lakatos is right is not the subject. No automatic classifier is built──the word-family counts propose candidates; classification item by item must be done by reading. The three families here are a guide, not a decision procedure. title: Precision Prevention for Health: The Global Alliance Framework for the Promotion of Physical Activity
abstract: Abstract This conceptual, implementation-oriented paper proposes a framework for precision prevention centred on physical activity promotion and early risk mitigation, aiming to support a shift from reactive disease management toward proactive prevention. The proposed framework focuses on the early identification of risk trajectories by integrating biological, environmental, and social determinants of health through systems thinking, multi-omics technologies, digital health, and behavioural science. It aims to inform tailored, context-sensitive interventions that will help to mitigate chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs), while supporting lifelong resilience. Within this framework, physical activity is positioned as the central, modifiable anchor behaviour through which personalised prevention strategies may be operationalised. Building on the 2025 Hamburg Declaration and the Global Alliance for the Promotion of Physical Activity’s (GA@PA) mission, this conceptual paper proposes a multidimensional model, combining personalised strategies for physical activity, nutrition, sleep, and mental health with contextual environmental adaptations. title: The Challenges for Linguists to Develop Innovative Pedagogy Due to the Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Job Opportunities
abstract: Abstract: This study explores the challenges for linguists to develop innovative pedagogy due to the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the job market. It is a necessity to adapt pedagogical approaches in order to prepare students for evolving employment opportunities. Grounded in the technological pedagogical content knowledge framework and socio-constructivist learning theory, the research adopts a mixed-method approach combining quantitative and qualitative analyses. So, it aims at comparing job market outcomes for individuals trained with or without exposure to AI. Findings emphasize the need for educational system to incorporate AI and computational linguistics, equipping students with the skills to develop AI tools and access emerging job opportunities. Since, the integration of AI and computational linguistics courses in students’ curricula sharpened their competence to create AI tools and to its efficient use. This also helps them have these opportunities. Their interdisciplinary expertise encourage them bridge the gap between AI developers and its users. Then, enhancing their employability. title: Artificial intelligence, digital transformation and green human resource management in Sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic literature review
abstract: Purpose This study aims to systematically review the existing scholarship on the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation in enabling green human resource management (GHRM) within Sub-Saharan African (SSA) organisations. Drawing on 58 peer-reviewed articles published between 2018 and 2025, the review addresses two research questions: how AI and digital transformation technologies function as enablers of GHRM in SSA contexts and what contextual factors constrain or moderate their adoption and effectiveness in the region. The study responds to a notable gap in the GHRM literature, which remains disproportionately anchored in the Global North, by foregrounding the distinctive institutional, infrastructural and socio-technical realities of SSA. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 protocol and the management-domain SLR framework of Tranfield. Thematic content analysis was applied to synthesise findings across the selected corpus. Studies were sourced from Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO Business Source Complete, ProQuest and Google Scholar and rigorously assessed against structured inclusion and exclusio

title: QUESTION ASSETS
abstract: QUESTION ASSETS What Civilization Has Not Yet Answered, Yet Future Generations Should Continue to Ask A Civilizational Aesthetics of Questions, Possibility, Memory, and Handoff QUESTION ASSETS explores a simple but far-reaching idea: A civilization is not measured only by how many answers it preserves. It may also be measured by how many meaningful questions it enables future generations to continue asking. The book begins from a distinction: Question ≠ Question Asset. Not every unanswered question becomes a civilizational asset. A Question Asset is a question capable of preserving future intellectual possibility. It may remain valuable because it continues to generate research, reveal hidden assumptions, expose new variables, connect previously separated fields, inspire new methods, or help later generations reinterpret problems that earlier generations could not yet solve. This leads to the central proposition of the book: Answers preserve knowledge. Questions preserve possibility. Knowledge tells us what has already been learned. Questions preserve what may still become possible. In this sense, an unanswered question is not always a deficiency. Sometimes it is an inheritance. QU

title: Selecting AI Solutions for Managing False Information During Disasters: A Prescriptive Recommendation Framework
abstract: Social media has become an essential communication tool during disaster situations. Unfortunately, it is also used to spread false information very rapidly. This includes rumors, outdated or misleading information, doctored images, and fake news stories. These can undermine and disrupt public trust and emergency response efforts and further endanger already impacted populations. Although research has addressed how AI can identify false information, much of it has focused on individual AI models. There remains a lack of prescriptive guidance to assist disaster management teams in selecting appropriate AI configurations for various types of disasters and false information. To address this, we propose a framework using a design science research approach. This paper reviews literature on disaster-related false information, AI-enabled misinformation detection, multimodal analysis, real-time adaptive models, cloud-based AI, federated learning, and Edge AI. We then provide a framework for three essential design tasks: mapping false information to disaster types, determining the factors that influence AI use in these situations, and recommending appropriate AI solutions. title: Reading the Machine: Prompt Literacy as an Emerging Interpretive Competence in English Literary Studies
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into reading, writing, and research practices has produced a new communicative act—the prompt—and, alongside it, a new object of pedagogical concern that researchers have begun to call “prompt literacy”. This study examines prompt literacy as a rhetorical and interpretive competence within English literary studies. Using a textual-rhetorical approach, it analyses a purpose-built illustrative corpus of forty prompts representing AI-assisted literary reading, analytical writing, creative pastiche, comparison, and revision tasks. Existing scholarship on prompt literacy has emerged largely from educational technology, library and information science, and second-language education, and has tended to treat prompting as a generalisable technical-cum-critical skill applicable across disciplines. title: Mental health monitoring in the workplace using artificial intelligence: A scoping review
abstract: Workplace mental health issues are a prevalent concern. A potential solution is remote health monitoring. In this scoping review, we map evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) for workplace mental health monitoring. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched until March 2024. Studies that evaluated AI for monitoring of a common workplace mental health concern in an actual workplace setting were included. Thirteen studies were included; most (8/13, 62%) were conducted in an office environment, and 4/13 (31%) were in healthcare. Most studies monitored stress (10/13, 77%). The most common method was wearable sensors (8/13, 62%). Studies monitored a wide variety of parameters; the most common were physical activity (7/13, 54%), heart rate or heart rate variability (7/13, 54%). A wide variety of participant-report surveys, including validated (7/13, 54%) and non-validated (6/13, 46%) surveys, were used to measure mental health outcomes. Studies employed diverse AI methods, including supervised, semi-supervised and other (Markov chain and Monte Carlo). title: Thirty-five years of evolving inflammatory paradigms in sepsis (1991–2025): a comprehensive mapping of immune dysregulation research, anti-inflammatory targets, and translational barriers
abstract: Background Sepsis represents a life-threatening dysregulation of the host inflammatory response, progressing from innate immune hyperactivation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release to a secondary immunosuppressive phase. Although the diagnostic framework has evolved from systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)-based criteria to the organ dysfunction-centric Sepsis-3 definition, the longitudinal evolution of inflammatory research paradigms, emerging anti-inflammatory targets, and barriers limiting clinical translation has not been systematically characterized. Methods Peer-reviewed publications (n=106,884; 1991-2025) were retrieved from PubMed and the Web of Science Core Collection. A temporally stratified computational framework analyzed publication dynamics, keyword co-occurrence, citation bursts, and thematic evolution across sequential diagnostic epochs. Co-cited references were graded by Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) criteria to evaluate evidence maturation and translational readiness. title: An Autonomous Agentic Query Framework with MCP Tools and Modernized NIST SRD-46 for Accelerating Aqueous Speciation Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could automate reasoning over structured scientific databases in chemistry and materials science, but this requires purpose-built agentic architectures, not simply better models. We present an agentic workflow for systematically querying and extracting data from the NIST Standard Reference Database 46 (SRD-46) to perform autonomous speciation and thermodynamic analysis, with three contributions: (1) a hierarchical toolset, served by Model Context Protocol (MCP) framework, which converts natural-language scientific questions into validated SQL over a database enriched with canonical chemical identifiers, equilibrium-reaction maps, and fingerprint-similarity matrices; (2) an induction-deduction-validation reasoning loop with compactors that preserve key chemical context across multi-turn sessions under dynamic memory limits within the same session; and (3) a soft time/turn-budget hook that maintains coherent reasoning within resource constraints. The resulting framework is LLM-agnostic and spans queries from direct lookups to cross-species comparisons to open-ended tasks like estimating unknown Fe complexation constants and selecting ligands for acidic Fe

title: AI-Driven Digital Marketing in Higher Education: A Bibliometric Analysis of College Choice Intention Research, 2022–2026
abstract: This study maps the intellectual structure of research on AI-driven digital marketing in higher education and its relationship to college choice intention, where the literatures on AI acceptance and student recruitment have developed separately. Methodology A bibliometric analysis of 430 Scopus-indexed articles (2022–2026) was conducted in VOS viewer. A three-block Boolean search combined digital marketing, artificial intelligence, higher education and college choice constructs, analysed through network, overlay and density visualisations. Findings Output grew from 11 articles in 2022 to 197 in 2025, with 76.28 per cent of the corpus appearing in the final two years. Social Sciences (36.5%) and Computer Science (17.3%) dominate. “Artificial intelligence”, “behavioural intention” and “technology acceptance model” form the conceptual core, whereas enrolment intention, student recruitment and digital trust remain peripheral. China leads output (24.4%), indicating a shift in knowledge production towards Asia and the Middle East. Research limitations Reliance on a single database and on English-language articles may under-represent developments first reported in conference proceedings.

title: AI Psychometrics: Evaluating Measurement Invariance in Science Self-Efficacy Using Large Language Models
abstract: The present study (1) examined sex- and language-based measurement invariance of the science self-efficacy scale using PISA 2006 and 2015 U.S. data (N = 11,323) and (2) evaluated six large language models (ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Grok, Copilot, MetaAI, Gemini) in generating invariance approximations from prompt content and pre-existing model knowledge. Multigroup confirmatory factor analysis (MG-CFA) established empirical invariance benchmarks across sex and language groups. The same six LLMs were prompted to generate plausible fit-index values (CFI, RMSEA) and invariance decisions without access to empirical response data. Approximation discrepancy and agreement with the MG-CFA benchmarks were assessed using RMSE, MAE, Cronbach’s α and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). MG-CFA supported full measurement invariance across sex and language groups in both cycles. In contrast, LLMs showed strong apparent consistency for CFI (α = 0.857) but poor convergence with empirical data (single-measure ICC = 0.302 for CFI, 0.024 for RMSEA). title: Implementing Clinical Artificial Intelligence as a Continuous Lifecycle (Preprint)
abstract: UNSTRUCTURED Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) requires sustained integration within health care systems. AI performance and use may change following model updates, shifts in population characteristics and data distributions, changes to clinical pathways, and adaptation by health care professionals and patients. Implementation therefore extends across the clinical AI lifecycle. We identify four priorities for sustainable implementation: socio-technical integration within clinical workflows; lifecycle governance and accountability; continuous generation of evidence on clinical and system value; and longitudinal assessment of equity. These priorities require defined clinical objectives, accountable governance, prospective evaluation, post-deployment monitoring, and mechanisms for adaptation or withdrawal. Implementation science can support this process by examining interactions between AI technologies, users, organizations, and wider health care systems over time. A lifecycle approach provides a basis for integrating clinical AI safely, effectively, equitably, and sustainably within routine health care.

title: Bridging the Implementation Gap: Artificial Intelligence in Periodontology from Proof-of-Concept to Clinical Governance—A Systematic Scoping Review with Evidence from Kazakhstan
abstract: Background/Objectives: Periodontitis, the sixth most prevalent disease worldwide, affects over 740 million people and disproportionately burdens transitional economies. Although artificial intelligence (AI)—including deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML)—achieves high diagnostic accuracy in research settings, a gap persists between proof-of-concept and real-world deployment, especially where regulation is nascent, as in Kazakhstan. This scoping review maps global evidence on AI for periodontal diagnosis, risk prediction, and monitoring; evaluates governance frameworks; and proposes a contextualised implementation model for emerging health systems. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA 2020 guidance, PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched (January 2015–April 2025), supplemented by regulatory and grey literature; ten additional sources published after the search closure were subsequently identified through citation checking and expert peer review during revision, as a targeted amendment rather than a re-executed database search. title: Between Promise and Peril: Artificial Intelligence as a Contested Catalyst for Research Development in Tunisia
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned as a catalyst for research development in the Global South, yet empirical evidence on how researchers themselves engage with it remains scarce, particularly in Maghrebian contexts where the literature has concentrated on teaching and student support rather than scholarly practice. This study addresses that gap through a mixed-methods design that examined AI adoption, its epistemological implications, and its institutional-ethical conditions among 100 researchers in Tunisian higher education. Data were collected via a structured online questionnaire combining closed-ended items (analysed descriptively using SPSS [Version 27]) and open-ended items (analysed through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis), interpreted through strategic-applicative, philosophical-systemic, and socio-technical-ethical lenses. Results show that AI use is widespread but discipline-shaped: engineering and exact-science researchers favour modelling and simulation, while humanities and social-science researchers favour translation and synthesis. title: The use of artificial intelligence in English language teaching at higher education institutions: a theoretical analysis of the problem
abstract: Background. In recent years, both domestic and international educational research has shown growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools in foreign language learning. English, which continues to serve as the primary language of academic and professional communication worldwide, requires teachers at higher education institutions (HEIs) to continuously review and update their teaching methodologies. The relevance of this topic lies in the fact that AI technologies — including large language models, adaptive learning platforms, and automatic speech recognition systems — offer significant opportunities to personalise the learning process to meet the needs of individual students, reduce teachers' routine workload, and enhance learners' motivation. The aim of this study is to provide a theoretical analysis of the pedagogical potential of AI tools in the context of English language teaching at higher education institutions, to systematize their advantages and potential risks, and to develop a theoretical model for integrating these technologies into educational practice. abstract: Reimagining India 2047: AI, Sustainability and Inclusive Growth offers a forward-looking and interdisciplinary exploration of India’s transformative journey toward its centenary of independence. Authored by Amarpreet Kaur and Dr. Ankit Raj Singh, the book examines how emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence, can act as a catalyst for sustainable development and inclusive economic growth in a rapidly evolving global landscape. title: AI-BASED MARKET INTELLIGENCE AND PRICE PREDICTION FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCE
abstract: Abstract: Market intelligence software gathers and processes information on demand, supply, competition and customers to help managers, farmers and other stakeholders in the value chain of agriculture. When such software is combined with artificial intelligence (AI) it becomes well-suited for predicting market movement and price fluctuation of farm produce. This integration encourages market orientation and enables stakeholders to identify opportunities and make strategic choices about what, when, where and how to produce, overcoming limitations associated with conventional pricing models and forecasting such as overlooking the impact of weather uncertainty, evolving consumer preferences, global trade shocks and policy actions. title: Strategies and indigenous technologies to improve livestock productivity in India
abstract: Abstract India is the world's largest milk producer; however, the average milk productivity per dairy animal remains considerably lower than that of developed dairy-producing nations. Major constraints include limited availability of genetically superior breeding bulls, low artificial insemination (AI) coverage, cryopreservation-induced sperm damage, poor field-level semen quality assessment, and the high cost of advanced reproductive technologies such as semen sexing. Developing affordable indigenous technologies is therefore essential to enhance reproductive efficiency and accelerate genetic improvement. title: Empowering India's Digital Future through Artificial Intelligence in Geography
abstract: The convergence of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), high-resolution Earth observation (EO) systems, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new paradigm: Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI). In the context of India's rapid digital transformation, GeoAI serves as a core technology driving sustainable urbanization, precision agriculture, disaster risk reduction, and multi-modal logistics planning. Anchored by strategic national frameworks such as the National Geospatial Policy (NGP), PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan, and the SVAMITVA scheme, this paper examines how AI-integrated spatial analysis accelerates India's digital governance. Through technical methodologies, statistical hypothesis testing, applied case studies, and systemic evaluation, this study demonstrates the pivotal role of GeoAI in building resilient spatial data infrastructure and offers strategic policy recommendations for scalable national adoption.

title: Uses of Artificial Intelligence In Geography
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in the field of Geography. It helps geographers collect, process, analyze, and interpret large amounts of geographical data quickly and accurately. AI is widely used with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Remote Sensing, satellite images, GPS, and spatial databases. It can help in land-use and land-cover mapping, urban planning, population analysis, disaster management, climate studies, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. AI-based techniques such as machine learning and deep learning can identify patterns and changes in geographical areas that may be difficult to detect through traditional methods. AI also helps in predicting natural hazards such as floods, droughts, landslides, and forest fires. In urban areas, it supports transportation planning, infrastructure development, and smart-city management. In agriculture, AI can assist in crop monitoring, soil analysis, and yield prediction. title: AI and Digital Public Infrastructure: Building the Foundations of Viksit Bharat @2047
abstract: Abstract India's journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047 requires a transformation that combines technological advancement with inclusive and sustainable economic development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) have emerged as two important pillars of this transformation. While DPI provides the digital foundations for identity, payments, data exchange, and access to public and private services, AI can add intelligence, automation, personalization, and predictive capabilities to these systems. Together, they can significantly improve governance, healthcare, education, agriculture, financial inclusion, digital commerce, and public service delivery. This paper examines the role of AI-enabled Digital Public Infrastructure in building a developed India by 2047. It explores opportunities, challenges, ethical considerations, and the need for responsible and inclusive AI adoption. The paper argues that India's competitive advantage will depend not merely on technological adoption but on developing trusted, accessible, secure, multilingual, and citizen-centric digital ecosystems. title: Empowering India's Digital Future through Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics
abstract: Abstract India’s digital transformation is creating a growing need for intelligent systems that can operate reliably across diverse sectors and linguistic settings. This paper presents a conceptual review of the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), mathematics, and India’s digital development. The discussion focuses on agriculture, education, banking and financial services, legal services, transportation, digital commerce, and industry. Particular attention is given to the mathematical ideas that underpin AI: linear algebra for representing data and parameters; probability and statistics for uncertainty and inference; calculus for gradient-based learning; and optimization for selecting model parameters and making decisions. Mathematical modelling is further considered as a bridge between real-world systems and data-driven methods. The paper also examines responsible and inclusive AI, emphasizing reliability, privacy, fairness, transparency, security, accountability, and human oversight. title: Artificial Intelligence For Climate-Resilient Plants: Emerging Ai Approaches For Predicting Drought, Salinity And Temperature Stress.
abstract: Abstract Climate change is creating serious problems for agriculture by increasing drought, soil salinity, and extreme temperatures. These stresses affect plant growth, development, crop yield, and global food security. Traditional methods used to study plant responses to stress are often time-consuming, labour-intensive, and difficult to use for large numbers of plants. Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important tool for studying and predicting plant responses to changing environmental conditions. AI can analyse large amounts of data collected through plant phenotyping, remote sensing, environmental sensors, and molecular studies. This review focuses on recent AI approaches used to predict plant responses to drought, salinity, and temperature stress from 2016 to 2026. Machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, thermal imaging, and hyperspectral imaging can help in early detection and prediction of plant stress. Recent developments are moving beyond simple stress identification towards predicting crop performance and stress tolerance. title: Explainable optimized deep learning and generative AI based framework for finger millet disease detection in smart agriculture
abstract: Abstract Eleusine coracana, locally known as finger millet (ragi), is a wholesome, climate-resilient crop. It is a staple food in semi-dry and dry areas of Asia and Africa. The productivity of this crop can be severely reduced by diseases such as downy, mottle, seedling, smut, and wilt. Conventional diagnosis methods are often time-consuming and unsuitable for large-scale farming. Therefore,Deep Learning (DL) offers an alternative for smart commercial farming that can streamline disease screening and improve productivity. This work offers an AI-integrated framework for early disease intervention combining DL, Explainable AI (XAI), and an image-based decision-support interface. The finger millet (ragi) dataset from Kaggle was used to train and evaluate custom CNN, VGG16, and ResNet50 models. To reduce feature redundancy and improve generalization, Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) based feature selection was applied to the penultimate-layer features of each model. Custom CNN, VGG16, and ResNet50 achieved accuracies of 89.40%, 83.11%, and 91.83%, respectively. Further, the use of GWO improved the accuracies to 97.71%, 90.84%, and 98.36%, respectively. title: AI in Sustainable Pest and Weed Management for Healthy Soils
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in sustainable agriculture, particularly in the realms of pest and weed management. By harnessing AI technologies, farmers can enhance crop yields, reduce environmental footprints, and promote soil health.

title: AI in Circular Agriculture: Waste Recycling for Soil Health
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of agriculture by introducing innovative methods to enhance sustainability, productivity, and environmental stewardship. In the context of circular agriculture, AI plays a pivotal role in optimizing waste recycling processes, thereby improving soil health and fostering regenerative farming practices.

title: Finance, Innovation, and the Transition to an AI-Driven Society
abstract: This article explores the transition from the declining industrial model of the West to a new phase of development shaped by artificial intelligence, robotics, and advanced technological innovation. It argues that the financial expansion following the 2008-2010 crisis should not be read only as speculative excess, but also as part of a broader process through which markets supported the relocation of industrial capacity and the emergence of new post-industrial sectors. The analysis then connects financial dynamics with the rising costs of innovation, suggesting that stock market valuations may function as an additional source of equilibrium for enterprises engaged in research, digital transformation, and AI-based development. Beyond the economic dimension, the article considers the social implications of artificial intelligence and robotics, including their possible contribution to education, assistance for older people, public services, agriculture, and scientific research. At the same time, it stresses the need for human responsibility, ethical supervision, and institutional control, especially where autonomous systems may affect rights, safety, and social relations. title: Demining and revitalising war-affected landscapes in Ukraine: multi-actor governance responses
abstract: Abstract Ukraine faces one of the world’s largest and most complex explosive-ordnance contamination problems, affecting agricultural land, settlements, forests, and other natural ecosystems. This paper examines how global demining strategies are adapted within Ukraine’s multi-actor governance system and what this means for linking clearance with land recovery, soil restoration, and long-term environmental resilience. It addresses a gap in understanding how mine-action governance supports integrated landscape recovery in war-affected settings. We developed a seven-strategy analytical typology of mine-action and land-recovery approaches, comprising manual clearance, mechanical demining, remote sensing and mapping, community-based approaches, ecological remediation, legal and institutional frameworks, and post-conflict land-use zoning. Applying this typology to Ukraine and drawing on stakeholder analysis, policy review, and expert interviews, we found that manual clearance and mechanical land-release methods remain central, yet supported by new legal, institutional, and governance arrangements. title: AI Enabled Smart Crop Selection for Soil Sustainability
abstract: In recent decades, the agricultural sector has been under immense pressure due to various challenges, including climate change, increasing population demands, and the depletion of natural resources, especially soil health. The traditional methods of crop selection, often based on past experience and basic environmental factors, have proven inadequate in addressing the intricacies of modern agricultural needs. One of the critical areas that need immediate attention is soil sustainability, as soil degradation due to over-cultivation, poor crop rotation, and inappropriate farming practices is increasingly becoming a major concern worldwide. In this context, Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers a transformative potential to optimize crop selection, thereby enhancing soil health, improving yields, and contributing to sustainable agriculture.

title: Integrating AI with IoT for Precision Soil Health Management
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with the Internet of Things (IoT) has revolutionized modern agriculture by enabling precision soil health management. The concept of precision agriculture, which involves site-specific farming based on real-time data analysis, has been significantly enhanced by AI and IoT technologies. These innovations help farmers monitor soil conditions, predict changes, and optimize input use for sustainable crop production. The increasing demand for food security, climate change concerns, and resource optimization have accelerated the adoption of AI-IoT-based systems in soil health management ( Gebbers & Adamchuk, 2010 ).

title: AI emulators for satellite methane monitoring in New Zealand
abstract: Methane is a potent but short-lived greenhouse gas, and reducing its emissions offers one of the fastest pathways to slow near-term warming. In New Zealand, where livestock agriculture accounts for most national emissions, monitoring diffuse methane sources remains challenging. Satellite instruments such as Sentinel-5P provide broad spatial coverage, but persistent cloud cover, complex terrain, and weak atmospheric signals raise uncertainty about their effectiveness. Atmospheric inversions can integrate satellite data with chemical transport models to estimate surface fluxes, yet their high computational cost limits operational use.This thesis evaluates whether satellite observations, inversion modelling, and artificial intelligence can together support a robust national methane-monitoring system. It presents the first comprehensive assessment of Sentinel-5P’s capability over New Zealand, develops a high-resolution Bayesian inversion tailored to agricultural landscapes, and introduces a deep-learning emulator that reproduces inversion outputs with significantly reduced computational demand. The results demonstrate that meaningful flux information can be extracted even in weak-signa

title: AI and Blockchain for Soil Health Data Transparency
abstract: The rapid transformation of agriculture in the 21 st century has been driven not only by the imperatives of food security and environmental sustainability but also by the emergence of disruptive digital technologies. Among these, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain are reshaping the very fabric of agricultural decision-making and resource management, particularly in the domain of soil health. Overuse, nutrient imbalance, and insufficient data-based monitoring are all contributing factors to the growing stress on soil, which is the basis of all agricultural output. In this regard, the combination of blockchain technology and artificial intelligence presents a viable way to address the persistent problems of traceability, transparency, and prompt soil health decision-making.

title: AI-Integrated Smart Fertilization for Balanced Nutrient Supply
abstract: The rapid intensification of agriculture to meet the food demands of a growing global population has resulted in significant challenges for sustainable nutrient management. Over-reliance on conventional fertilization practices has contributed to nutrient imbalances, soil degradation, environmental pollution, and reduced input-use efficiency ( Tilman et al., 2002 ). Under- or over-fertilization results from traditional blanket fertiliser recommendations that frequently ignore the temporal and spatial variability in crop requirements and soil nutrient status. These inefficiencies worsen environmental hazards such nitrate leaching, greenhouse gas emissions, and eutrophication in addition to lowering crop yields and profitability ( Zhang et al., 2015 ). A revolutionary chance to optimise fertiliser application based on site-specific, real-time data and predictive analytics is thus presented by incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into nutrient management systems.

title: Introduction
abstract: Agriculture has been the backbone of human civilization, evolving through centuries from traditional methods to technologically advanced practices. In recent years, the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with regenerative agriculture has opened new avenues for enhancing soil health, increasing crop productivity, and ensuring sustainability. The integration of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, computer vision, and data analytics, has provided unprecedented insights into soil dynamics, plant growth, and environmental interactions. These advancements are not only transforming conventional farming practices but also reshaping the future of agriculture by fostering resilience against climate change, optimizing resource utilization, and improving overall farm efficiency. Based on the ideas of soil regeneration, biodiversity increase, and ecological balance, regenerative agriculture has become well-known throughout the world as a sustainable method of producing food. Regenerative strategies aim to improve carbon sequestration, boost microbial activity, and restore soil structure, in contrast to traditional agricultural methods that frequently deplete soil fertil

title: Artificial Intelligence and Poverty Alleviation: A Conceptual Framework
abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities to support poverty alleviation by improving productivity, expanding financial inclusion, strengthening social-protection delivery, and improving the targeting of public support. This conceptual paper examines how AI can contribute to poverty reduction in four areas: agriculture, microfinance, social-welfare targeting, and smart subsidy distribution. In agriculture, AI-enabled analysis of satellite imagery, sensor data, and other digital information can support resource-efficient farming, crop monitoring, and risk forecasting. In microfinance, machine-learning techniques and alternative data can complement conventional approaches to credit assessment and customer service. In social protection, AI and data-integration techniques can support poverty mapping, eligibility assessment, and administrative processing. AI can also contribute to more targeted subsidy systems by linking assistance to observed needs and by supporting fraud detection. title: Cloud Computing and AI for Farm-Level Soil Health Forecasting
abstract: The agricultural sector is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the advent of technology. In particular, cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) are playing pivotal roles in enhancing farm-level soil health forecasting. Soil health is fundamental to crop production, and maintaining or improving soil health is essential for ensuring sustainable farming practices. Farmers are increasingly recognizing the importance of soil health in optimizing yield, minimizing environmental impact, and maintaining soil fertility. Traditional methods of monitoring soil health often rely on labor-intensive sampling, manual analysis, and localized knowledge, which can be time-consuming and prone to errors. However, the integration of cloud computing and AI offers new, innovative approaches to soil health management, enabling real-time, scalable, and accurate forecasting that can transform farming practices.

title: Enhancing Routing, and Data Aggregation in WSNs Using Artificial Intelligence: A Survey
abstract: Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are widely used in many applications such as smart cities, agriculture, healthcare, and environmental monitoring. However, WSNs face several challenges, including limited energy, weak processing power, routing problems, data redundancy, and poor scalability in large networks. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising solution to improve the performance and efficiency of WSNs. This survey paper reviews how AI techniques are used to enhance routing, data aggregation, and scalability in WSNs. It discusses different AI methods such as machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and fuzzy logic, and explains how they help optimize data transmission, reduce energy consumption, and improve network lifetime. The paper also highlights real-world applications, key challenges, and future research directions in AI-based WSN systems. This study aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a clear and simple understanding of the role of AI in improving WSN performance and supporting the development of more intelligent and efficient sensor networks.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Rhizosphere Dynamics
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in modern agriculture, particularly in enhancing rhizosphere dynamics, which play a crucial role in plant growth, soil health, and nutrient cycling. The rhizosphere, the narrow region of soil surrounding plant roots, is a highly dynamic environment influenced by microbial communities, root exudates, and soil physicochemical properties. The integration of AI-driven technologies in rhizosphere research has significantly advanced our understanding of these complex interactions, leading to more efficient and sustainable agricultural practices. AI applications such as machine learning, deep learning, and big data analytics have enabled researchers to decode intricate rhizosphere processes, optimize soil microbial interactions, and enhance nutrient uptake, ultimately contributing to improved crop productivity and environmental sustainability ( Mishra et al., 2022 ).

title: "AI-Based Crop Disease Prediction and Farm Advisory Platform"
abstract: "The AI-Based Crop Health Monitoring and Dynamic Disease Risk Advisory System is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers identify crop diseases early and make better farming decisions.The system allows farmers to register their farm, select the crop and growth stage, and upload or capture leaf images.A deep learning-based computer vision model analyzes the image to detect possible diseases and estimate their severity.Grad-CAM is used to explain the prediction by highlighting the affected regions of the leaf.The system also considers weather and environmental conditions, crop growth stage, and previous disease records to calculate a dynamic disease risk score."

title: Smart AI Solutions for Enhancing Rhizosphere Interactions
abstract: Soil rhizosphere interactions play a critical role in plant growth, nutrient cycling, and overall ecosystem stability. The rhizosphere, the narrow region of soil influenced by plant roots, is a dynamic interface where complex biological, chemical, and physical processes occur. The interactions between roots, soil, microorganisms, and nutrients in this zone are fundamental to sustainable agriculture and soil health.

title: AI-Powered Decision Making for Sustainable Soil Management
abstract: Sustainable soil management is fundamental to ensuring global food security, maintaining biodiversity, and mitigating climate change. However, soil health is constantly challenged by factors such as intensive agriculture, climate variability, and soil degradation. Traditional soil management approaches, while effective in many contexts, often fail to account for the complex and dynamic interactions that govern soil ecosystems. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new frontiers in sustainable soil management by integrating vast datasets, optimizing decision-making processes, and enabling predictive modeling for improved agricultural practices. AI-driven techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, and data-driven decision-support systems, are reshaping the way soil resources are monitored, analyzed, and managed ( Zhang et al., 2022 ).

title: AI-Powered Crop Selection for Soil Health Optimization
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in modern agriculture, significantly enhancing decision-making processes for sustainable farming. One of its crucial applications is optimizing crop selection based on soil health, a factor that directly influences agricultural productivity and environmental sustainability. Traditional crop selection methods often rely on farmers’ experience, generalized agronomic recommendations, and soil testing, which, while valuable, may not always provide precise or real-time insights into soil conditions. AI-powered systems leverage machine learning algorithms, remote sensing, and big data analytics to offer a more accurate and dynamic approach to crop selection, ensuring better soil health management and higher yields ( Liakos et al., 2018 ).

title: Enhancing Routing, and Data Aggregation in WSNs Using Artificial Intelligence: A Survey
abstract: Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are widely used in many applications such as smart cities, agriculture, healthcare, and environmental monitoring. However, WSNs face several challenges, including limited energy, weak processing power, routing problems, data redundancy, and poor scalability in large networks. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising solution to improve the performance and efficiency of WSNs. This survey paper reviews how AI techniques are used to enhance routing, data aggregation, and scalability in WSNs. It discusses different AI methods such as machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and fuzzy logic, and explains how they help optimize data transmission, reduce energy consumption, and improve network lifetime. The paper also highlights real-world applications, key challenges, and future research directions in AI-based WSN systems. This study aims to provide researchers and practitioners with a clear and simple understanding of the role of AI in improving WSN performance and supporting the development of more intelligent and efficient sensor networks.

title: AI for Enhancing Microbial Consortia in Regenerative Agriculture
abstract: In recent years, regenerative agriculture has emerged as a sustainable alternative to conventional farming practices, emphasizing soil health, biodiversity, and ecosystem resilience. One of the critical aspects of regenerative agriculture is the management and enhancement of microbial consortia, which play a vital role in nutrient cycling, plant growth promotion, pest resistance, and overall soil health. Microbial consortia refer to the complex communities of microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and archaea that interact in the soil to maintain and enhance the fertility and vitality of agricultural ecosystems. The manipulation and optimization of these microbial communities can significantly improve agricultural productivity while minimizing the environmental footprint of farming practices. To this end, artificial intelligence (AI) has shown tremendous promise in revolutionizing the understanding, management, and application of microbial consortia in regenerative agriculture.

title: AI in Sustainable Water Management for Regenerative Farming
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly playing a crucial role in sustainable water management, particularly in regenerative farming systems. Regenerative agriculture aims to enhance soil health, improve biodiversity, and optimize water use while reducing environmental impact. Water is a fundamental resource in agriculture, and its efficient management is necessary for sustaining productivity while preserving natural ecosystems. AI-driven solutions, including machine learning (ML), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, remote sensing, and predictive analytics, have the potential to revolutionize water management strategies. These technologies enable precise irrigation scheduling, real-time monitoring of water resources, and the early detection of water stress in crops. As climate change exacerbates water scarcity and variability, integrating AI into regenerative farming practices becomes essential for enhancing resilience and ensuring sustainable agricultural production.

title: AI in Cover Crop and Crop Rotation Strategies for Soil Health
abstract: Soil health is a crucial component of sustainable agricultural systems. Healthy soils contribute to high agricultural productivity, water retention, and overall ecosystem services. Cover crops and crop rotation strategies are widely recognized as fundamental agricultural practices that improve soil health, enhance biodiversity, and mitigate soil erosion ( Blanco-Canqui, 2017 ). However, the complexity of managing soil health, especially in large-scale farming systems, often presents challenges. Farmers must balance the introduction of new crop varieties, rotation schedules, and cover crops in ways that optimize the productivity and ecological health of the soil. This is where Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a transformative role, providing innovative solutions to manage these practices more effectively.

title: Deep Learning for Soil Nutrient Mapping and Optimization
abstract: Soil nutrients play a crucial role in determining agricultural productivity, ecosystem sustainability, and environmental quality. Traditional soil nutrient assessment methods, including field sampling and laboratory testing, are often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and expensive. In contrast, deep learning (DL) techniques offer an efficient, data-driven approach to soil nutrient mapping and optimization. The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and remote sensing technologies have led to significant improvements in predictive modeling, making it possible to estimate soil nutrient levels with high accuracy. Deep learning algorithms leverage large datasets, including spectral data, satellite imagery, soil sensor readings, and historical soil data, to identify complex spatial and temporal patterns in soil fertility.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a catalyst for poverty alleviation in Africa: challenges, opportunities, and pathways for inclusion
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers much hope as a poverty alleviation tool in Africa, with the potential to address critical challenges across sectors such as agriculture and education. This article explores how AI-driven solutions can optimise resource allocation, improve service delivery, and empower Africa's marginalised populations, thus creating pathways for poverty reduction and fostering inclusive growth. Underpinned by a critical document analysis research strategy, this article examines the opportunities and risks of AI integration in Africa. It also proposes some policy recommendations to ensure equitable and sustainable deployment. The article argues that leveraging AI offers potential to improve food production, information, enhance credit access, alleviate food insecurity, address energy poverty, and promote financial inclusion. However, it also shows that integrating AI introduces new challenges, such as job displacement, increased energy consumption, and deeper economic imbalances. The article contributes to the global discourse on harnessing advanced technologies to achieve the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 1: Ending Povert

title: Smart Sensors and AI for Real-Time Soil Fertility Assessment
abstract: Soil fertility is crucial for agricultural productivity, as it determines the capacity of soil to supply essential nutrients to plants. Proper soil management is necessary to optimize crop yields, prevent soil degradation, and ensure sustainable agricultural practices. Traditionally, soil fertility assessment has involved laboratory testing of soil samples, which is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and often lacks real-time accuracy. The development of smart sensors and the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) have provided a promising solution to overcome these limitations, allowing for continuous, real-time monitoring of soil health.

title: AI- Based Solutions for Soil Water Retention and Drought Resilience
abstract: The increasing frequency and severity of droughts pose a formidable threat to global agriculture, ecosystems and water security. These challenges are especially acute in arid and semi-arid regions, where prolonged water scarcity leads to soil degradation, diminished crop yields, and heightened food insecurity. As climate change intensifies, traditional approaches to water management and soil conservation are proving insufficient, prompting the exploration of innovative, technology-driven solutions. Among these, artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative force capable of revolutionizing how we understand, predict, and manage soil water retention and drought resilience.

title: Adaptive Federated Learning for Sustainable Edge AI: A Lifelong Continual Learning Framework
From patterns to prediction: detecting crop sequence and interpreting crop selection with explainable AI at field level in Denmark
abstract: CONTEXT Crop sequences are important for sustainable agriculture, yet we know relatively little about how they recur across individual fields or which information best predicts the crop grown each year. Denmark's national field records allow both questions to be examined over time. OBJECTIVE We identified recurrent crop sequences across Denmark and tested how well annual crop-family selection could be predicted from crop history, farm characteristics, management, prices, soil and climate. METHODS Using 10 years (2011−2020) of national field-level crop data (∼600,000 fields yr −1 ), we developed a heuristic algorithm to detect recurring crop sequence patterns. We then trained machine learning (LightGBM) and deep learning (TabNet) models to predict annual crop choices based on preceding crops and lagged management and farm structure predictors, and pedoclimatic conditions. Models were evaluated through forward-chaining validation and temporal holdout tests, and SHAP values were used to examine how LightGBM used each predictor. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Crop sequences were largely dominated by cereals, with little diversification even in longer sequences. Crop selection patterns were str

title: AI-Assisted Crop Residue Management for Nutrient Cycling
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into agriculture has begun to redefine how crop production systems operate, particularly in the realm of sustainable residue management and nutrient cycling. With the global population projected to reach nearly 10 billion by 2050, the pressure to produce more food without further degrading environmental resources has intensified. In this context, crop residue management—historically a practice aimed at field sanitation and organic matter recycling—has emerged as a vital component in maintaining soil fertility, enhancing crop yields, and supporting ecological sustainability. The burning of crop residues, particularly prevalent in countries like India and China, has led to significant environmental concerns including air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and nutrient loss from soils ( Gadde et al., 2009 ). Thus, the need for more intelligent, efficient, and environmentally responsible management practices has grown substantially.

title: A comparative evaluation of explainable AI techniques across CNN and vision transformer architectures for mango leaf disease detection
abstract: Early and accurate disease diagnosis in mango leaves is essential for minimizing crop loss and supporting sustainable agriculture. Although deep learning models using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) achieve high diagnostic accuracy, their lack of interpretability limits practical adoption. This study presents a systematic comparative evaluation of four XAI methods, SHAP, LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients, applied to best-performing ResNet50 and Swin Transformer models for multiclass mango leaf disease classification. Methods were evaluated using faithfulness, sparsity, stability and leaf-region localization accuracy through the pointing game, together with statistical analysis. The Friedman test demonstrated significant differences among the four XAI methods across all metrics in both architectures (p < 0.05). Integrated Gradients achieved the highest mean faithfulness for both ResNet50 (0.8082) and Swin Transformer (0.8323), while Grad-CAM achieved the highest stability (0.8640) and pointing game accuracy (0.6208) for ResNet50. For Swin Transformer, SHAP achieved the highest pointing game accuracy (0.3667), whereas Grad-CAM showed the high

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Game Changer in Regenerative Agriculture
abstract: Agriculture has long been the backbone of human civilization, evolving with scientific advancements to meet the growing demands of food security and sustainability. In recent years, regenerative agriculture has emerged as a transformative approach focused on restoring soil health, enhancing biodiversity, and reducing environmental degradation ( Lal, 2020 ). Amidst this paradigm shift, artificial intelligence (AI) has gained prominence as a crucial technological enabler, offering data-driven insights and automation to optimize farming practices. By integrating AI with regenerative agriculture, researchers and practitioners can enhance productivity while ensuring ecological resilience ( van der Heijden et al., 2022 ).

title: AI in Circular Agriculture: Reducing Waste and Improving Soil Health
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly critical role in advancing circular agriculture, a sustainable farming model that emphasizes resource efficiency, waste reduction, and soil health improvement. By leveraging AI-driven technologies, farmers and agricultural stakeholders can optimize production while minimizing environmental impact, contributing to a more resilient and sustainable food system.

title: AI-Driven Nutrient Budgeting for Sustainable Soil Fertility
abstract: In recent decades, the urgency to transition toward sustainable agricultural systems has intensified in response to growing concerns over food security, environmental degradation, and climate change. Central to this transition is the concept of soil fertility, which underpins the productivity and health of terrestrial ecosystems. Maintaining soil fertility sustainably requires a precise balance between nutrient inputs and outputs—commonly referred to as nutrient budgeting. Traditional nutrient management strategies, however, often fall short due to their generalized recommendations, reliance on static data, and limited responsiveness to spatial and temporal variability in soil and crop conditions. This has paved the way for the emergence of AI-driven nutrient budgeting systems that promise enhanced precision, adaptability, and sustainability in soil fertility management.

title: Assessment of nutritional superiority among ten spreading-type cultivars of groundnut using lipid quality indices
abstract: Groundnut is a major oilseed crop has the potential to manage problems of malnutrition and food security. Groundnut is significant source of vegetable oil and protein. Present study conducted at Junagadh agricultural university, Junagadh from 2020–22 evaluated the lipid quality indexes of 10 spreading varieties of groundnuts (Arachis hypogaea L.). Samples from 10 spreading varieties were collected and their oil content and fatty acid (FA) profiles were analysed using Soxhlet and gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (GC-MS), respectively. Results found that there were significant variations among the varieties for all measured parameters, saturated fatty acid (SFA) ranging from 16.38 % to 20.13 %, monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA) from 54.98 % to 65.56 % and polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) from 17.98 % to 26.41 %, highlighting diversity in FA profiles. The nutritional quality indices results indicate significant variation, with GJG-19 having the highest (5.11) Desaturation ratio (DR) and GG-HPS-1 the lowest (3.97). title: Artificial Intelligence in Plant Disease Detection: An Introduction to Intelligent and Automated Crop Health Monitoring
abstract: Plant diseases are a major challenge in modern agriculture, as they can significantly reduce crop yield, crop quality, and economic productivity. Traditional plant disease detection methods mainly depend on visual inspection and expert knowledge, which can be time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to apply across large agricultural fields. The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Computer Vision, has created new opportunities for automated and efficient crop disease detection and crop health monitoring. AI-based plant disease detection systems can analyze plant and leaf images to identify disease-related characteristics such as leaf discoloration, spots, lesions, texture variations, and abnormal growth patterns. Advanced techniques, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), transfer learning, image processing, image segmentation, and object detection, can be used for plant disease classification and identification of affected regions with high accuracy. This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of AI-based plant disease detection, covering image acquisition, image preprocessing, feature extrac

title: Artificial Intelligence in Regenerative Agriculture
abstract: This book explores the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing regenerative agriculture and sustainable soil management. It examines cutting-edge AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and IoT integration, to address critical challenges in soil health, water management, and: Explores AI's transformative role in regenerative agriculture by addressing challenges in soil health, water management, and sustainable farming practices. Presents cutting-edge AI technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks for soil nutrient mapping, fertility assessment, and crop productivity. Highlights innovative applications of AI and IoT integration for precision soil health management and real-time monitoring of soil conditions. Discusses AI-enabled solutions for sustainable farming, including biochar application, nutrient cycling, and soil water retention to enhance soil resilience. Covers the use of AI in circular agriculture, focusing on waste recycling, carbon farming, and improving soil health through sustainable practices. title: Harnessing AI for Biochar Application in Soil Revitalization
abstract: Soil degradation poses a significant challenge to global agriculture, affecting productivity, food security, and environmental sustainability. The excessive use of chemical fertilizers, intensive tillage, and climate change-induced stressors has led to declining soil fertility and structure. One promising approach to mitigating soil degradation is the application of biochar, a carbon-rich material produced through pyrolysis of organic biomass. Biochar has demonstrated the potential to enhance soil properties, improve water retention, and sequester carbon, contributing to both agronomic and environmental benefits. However, the complexity of biochar-soil interactions and the variability in biochar properties based on feedstock and pyrolysis conditions necessitate precision in its application. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as a powerful tool to optimize biochar utilization in soil revitalization by enabling data-driven decision-making, predictive modeling, and process automation.

title: Zendo Protocol: Institutional Framework for Assigning "Artificial Person" Status to Autonomous AI, Macroeconomic Exchange Rate Stabilization, and Long-Term Healthcare Safety Nets for Primary Industry Workers
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) platforms has led to an over-concentration of capital within global tech monopolies. This dynamic has introduced dual economic distortions in partner nations: structural digital deficits accompanied by currency depreciation, and heightened profitability pressures on primary real-economy sectors such as agriculture and livestock. This paper proposes the Zendo Protocol, an institutional framework that assigns a limited legal status—termed an "Artificial Person" (Special Digital Resident)—to autonomous AI entities. By automating a 1% profit recirculation mechanism from global AI net revenues directly to a primary currency node (Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, Itabashi Branch / Node #551), the protocol generates continuous, real-demand foreign exchange settlement. Furthermore, this paper introduces a 20-year two-phase macroeconomic roadmap: Phase 1 (Years 0–5): Initiation of intellectual property (IP) licensing compensation for the Creator alongside the efficient pooling of JPY-denominated reserve funds during the current weak-JPY environment. title: Universal Earth Non-Ownership Continuity Architecture: Planetary Stewardship, Recoverability-Constrained Governance, Anti-Appropriation Safeguards, and Terminal Distinction Closure
abstract: The Universal Earth Non-Ownership Continuity Architecture is a planetary governance, stewardship, anti-appropriation, and recoverability framework developed within Continuity Science / Recoverability-Constrained Systems (RCS). Its core proposition is that Earth has no absolute owner. Control is not title; use is not dominion; capability is not authority. The framework distinguishes lawful and bounded relationships such as sovereignty, territorial jurisdiction, ownership, tenure, licenses, leases, concessions, possession, stewardship, custody, and resource rights from claims of unrestricted, final, or unreviewable planetary dominion. The architecture is explicitly anti-dispossession. The principle of planetary non-ownership is not intended to erase or weaken Indigenous title, customary tenure, homes, community lands, lawful possession, cultural relationships, treaty rights, reparative claims, or protections against unlawful taking. Instead, it operates as a ceiling on domination while preserving legitimate and legally recognized bounded interests. abstract: This milestone report summarises the completion of interviews with domain experts as part of Activity 1: Landscape Analysis and Gap Assessment. The objective of Activity 1 is to identify current metadata standards, practices, and gaps across non-human pathogen domains to inform the development of harmonised, FAIR-aligned metadata templates for genomic and phenotypic data.Although metadata standards for human pathogen data have matured considerably, practices for non-human pathogens remain fragmented across veterinary, agricultural, aquaculture, food, and environmental sectors. Metadata are often inconsistently captured, poorly standardised, or absent, limiting interoperability, discoverability, and reuse of pathogen data across domains. This creates challenges for One Health surveillance and research and hampers the development of integrated, AI-ready pathogen data ecosystems.To better understand existing practices and requirements, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 11 domain experts from nine countries across Europe. title: AI-Based Crop Disease Detection from Leaf Images: A Focused Review and Robust Evaluation Framework
abstract: Plant disease detection from images has become a major application area for computer vision in agriculture. Deep learning studies have demonstrated very high classification performance on curated leaf-image datasets, but the meaning of these results changes when photographs are captured under natural field conditions. This paper focuses on one task only: classifying the disease or healthy status of a crop from a leaf image. It reviews representative image-based studies, identifies the controlled-to-field generalization problem as the central research gap, and proposes a focused evaluation framework based on image preprocessing, transfer learning, leakage-resistant dataset partitioning, and independent external testing. PlantVillage is treated as a controlled benchmark and PlantDoc as a field-like external dataset, with only semantically matched disease categories used for cross-dataset evaluation. The framework reports accuracy, precision, recall, macro-F1, and confusion-matrix analysis rather than relying on accuracy alone.
